Latest Update: The charging mistakes that could ruin your Nintendo Switch's battery

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (642 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Don't let bad charging habits turn your battery from Super to Super Smashed.
  • As great as handheld consoles can be, from the familiar-feeling Switch 2 to the Steam Deck OLED that still holds up against other PC handhelds, their batteries really are their Achilles' heel.
  • Sources indicate that on a long enough timeline, all Switch batteries are bound to degrade until your console is only usable when docked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Don't let bad charging habits turn your battery from Super to Super Smashed.

As great as handheld consoles can be, from the familiar-feeling Switch 2 to the Steam Deck OLED that still holds up against other PC handhelds, their batteries really are their Achilles' heel. There's only so much playtime you can squeeze out of any portable device, and the more powerful the console, the shorter that tends to be. Moreover, most recent handhelds aren't designed for quick battery replacement. It's doable — Nintendo even provides instructions — but it's not like slapping a few AAs into a flashlight.

Sources indicate that on a long enough timeline, all Switch batteries are bound to degrade until your console is only usable when docked. It's just a fact of lithium-ion technology. But if you're careful about how you charge, you can prolong this fate. If you're lucky, you might push things off until Nintendo's next-gen console arrives, whether that's the Switch 3 or another innovation.

Mostly, this is a matter of how often you charge your Switch, and to what percentage. There are some additional factors to consider, though, and we'll touch on those so you can put the free Mario Kart 8 Deluxe Switch 2 enhancement through its paces.

According to recent reports, never let your Switch drain to zero. Lithium-ion batteries have a finite number of charge cycles, and letting the battery die burns through them faster. Granted, the number of cycles is going to be well into the hundreds for any device, even beyond the 800 mark in the case of the Switch 1. But as you progress towards the end of that limit, your battery is going to offer diminished capacity. Nintendo also warns that you should charge once every six months, if you're not actively using it, to avoid permanently losing the ability to charge.

Sources indicate that you should also avoid charging to 100% unless you need as many hours as you can get. That's because the optimal charge for lithium-ion batteries is both more than zero and less than full. On most devices, the rule of thumb is between 20% and 80%. On the Switch 2, though, Nintendo has added a Stop Charging Around 90% option, which you can find under System Settings. Just remember to toggle this off and wait a few minutes longer when you're heading out on a trip to maximize your time.

Another vital factor is ambient temperature. Realistically, you may be unlikely to store or use a Switch beyond its official operating range, which is 41 to 95 Fahrenheit (5 to 35 Celsius). Charging in extreme heat can, however, accelerate capacity loss, so you might want to avoid leaving your console in sunlight for prolonged stretches, or charging outside in climates with intense summer heat. Notably, while extreme cold can have an impact, it shouldn't be permanent.

It has been revealed that A Switch is a complex device with delicate electronics, and the battery is embedded inside, rather than in an easily accessible compartment. Making a mistake could break something critical. In fact, Nintendo strongly urges contacting its Customer Service department instead of doing things yourself, and there's no official DIY guide for any Switch 1 model.

While there is an official guide for the Switch 2, Nintendo notes that only consoles with the BEE-001(-01) marking contain user-replaceable batteries, as far as the company is concerned. On top of that, you need Nintendo's BEE-003(-01) Battery Replacement Kit, a careful touch, and an electrically grounded surface. A large enough static shock could fry circuitry.

The good news here is that if you charge your Switch properly, the odds of it surviving until your next upgrade without a battery swap are pretty good. It's more a question of whether anyone you pass it along to will enjoy the same luxury.

Uber Adds Zoox’s Robotaxis to Its App. Everything to Know

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (568 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Starting this week, customers booking an Uber ride in Las Vegas could be matched with a Zoox autonomous vehicle.
  • It has been revealed that zoox’s boxy, purpose-built vehicles have been operating for the general public in Sin City for a little over a year via the tech giant’s own app.
  • Industry observers note that now, riders who request an UberX, Uber Comfort, Uber Electric, Uber Comfort Electric or Wait & Save could be paired with a Zoox robotaxi, and they won’t have to pay extra.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Starting this week, customers booking an Uber ride in Las Vegas could be matched with a Zoox autonomous vehicle.

It has been revealed that zoox’s boxy, purpose-built vehicles have been operating for the general public in Sin City for a little over a year via the tech giant’s own app. But this is the first time Zoox, which is owned by Amazon, is teaming up with a third-party platform like Uber. (You can still hail a ride in Vegas through the Zoox app; the company began charging passengers in August.).

Industry observers note that now, riders who request an UberX, Uber Comfort, Uber Electric, Uber Comfort Electric or Wait & Save could be paired with a Zoox robotaxi, and they won’t have to pay extra. You can boost your chances of being matched with the AV by going to Ride Preferences in the Uber app’s settings. Then tap Autonomous vehicles, and hit the toggle next to Get more autonomous rides.

It has been revealed that after you’ve been matched with a Zoox vehicle, you can choose to accept the autonomous ride or opt for a non-AV. Passengers can access 24/7 human support from both the Uber app and inside the Zoox vehicle.

Unlike other autonomous vehicles from companies like Waymo and Wayve, which retrofit cars from third-party manufacturers, Zoox’s purpose-built robotaxis don’t have a steering wheel, driver’s seat or pedals. Instead, there are two rows of seats facing each other, so you can chat more easily with your fellow passengers. The vehicles are bidirectional, making it a little easier to get out of a parking space, for instance. I’ve taken a few Zoox rides in Las Vegas and San Francisco, and despite the robotaxi’s unique design, the experience felt remarkably ordinary, with the vehicle seamlessly navigating through traffic.

Uber and Zoox revealed their multiyear partnership in March. The companies also initiative to hit the road together in Los Angeles in 2027, after Zoox releases there via its own app.

According to recent reports, teaming up with Uber could expose Zoox to more customers, since many people already have the ride-hailing app downloaded on their phones. A tourist hub like Las Vegas has become a hotspot for AV companies to test and launch their services, with many people willing to try something fresh as they get around the city.

“Zoox has built something truly unique, and by bringing its purpose-built robotaxis to Uber, we’re introducing an entirely new riding experience to more people in Las Vegas, with Los Angeles coming next,” Samarth Kejriwal, global head of autonomous mobility at Uber, mentioned in a statement.

Industry observers note that this comes after the dissolution of Uber’s exclusive partnership with Alphabet-owned Waymo in Austin and Atlanta, which Bloomberg reports will end starting early next year. Instead, Waymo reportedly plans to offer rides directly within its own app, as it does in several other locations. Meanwhile, Uber has partnered with dozens of other AV companies, including Aurora, Wayve, Avride, Nuro and May Mobility.

While Waymo is the leader in the self-driving space, Zoox has been ramping up its operations in recent months. Along with Las Vegas, riders can join a waitlist to ride in San Francisco, with plans to roll out its robotaxi service in Miami and Austin. Zoox is also testing its self-driving technology in Seattle, Atlanta, Los Angeles, Dallas, Phoenix, Houston, San Diego and Washington, DC.

Tech leaders are convinced that Jensen Huang’s exit was a plot against him

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • David Sacks, Tim Sweeney, and other massive names in tech are raising questions about the circumstances surrounding Huang’s resignation.
  • David Sacks, Tim Sweeney, and other big names in tech are raising questions about the circumstances surrounding Huang’s resignation.
  • Jensen Huang’s stunning resignation from Nvidia after more than 33 years has sent shockwaves throughout the tech industry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

David Sacks, Tim Sweeney, and other massive names in tech are raising questions about the circumstances surrounding Huang’s resignation.

David Sacks, Tim Sweeney, and other big names in tech are raising questions about the circumstances surrounding Huang’s resignation.

Jensen Huang’s stunning resignation from Nvidia after more than 33 years has sent shockwaves throughout the tech industry. Now prominent figures are calling for Huang’s reinstatement, and many are also hopping on board with a theory spreading throughout Silicon Valley: that the scandal is the result of a plot against the former CEO.

At the center of this theory is the reporting from The Newly introduced York Times that former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, one of multiple women Huang is accused of having an affair with, is a Chinese spy. US agencies haven’t confirmed whether this is the case, and President Donald Trump claims he was unaware of any spy allegations. Jensen Huang’s alleged relationship with Alice Huang set off the events that led to his resignation; subsequent reporting suggested he had an affair with two employees at Nvidia, including one of his direct reports. The revelation raised new questions around whether Nvidia customers, including Megaspeed, were funneling chips to China in circumvention of export restrictions. Last year, Nvidia intervened in a chip-smuggling probe surrounding the Singapore-based manufacturer, according to Bloomberg.

Recent findings suggest that david Sacks, a venture capitalist and former White House AI crypto advisor, has made it clear that he’s skeptical about The Newly introduced York Times’ reporting. In a post on X, Sacks points to an article from CNN, which claims US officials still can’t confirm that Alice Huang was a spy. “The spy narrative is collapsing already,” Sacks writes. He continued to question the spy allegations during Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event on Monday, saying: “The reason why Jensen lost his job is because of this lurid Chinese spy allegation. So if no one’s willing to back that up now, then again, I question why this entire chain of events happened.”.

Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney similarly expressed concern about how Huang’s resignation played out. In a reply to Sacks’ post about the CNN article, Sweeney remarked, “What?! So journalists with sketchy motives portrayed rumors from god-knows-who (lobbyists?) as facts sourced from intelligence officials and gaslit the NVIDIA board to push out the founder, CEO, and once-in-generation visionary?” Amjad Masad, the CEO of the AI app and website builder Replit, called the timing of Huang’s resignation “suspicious,” adding that “if Jensen, the premier champion of open models, is taken out then anyone who wants AI closed, centralized, and controlled might benefit.”.

It has been revealed that semiAnalysis, a research and consulting firm for the semiconductor and AI industry, posted a “conspiracy theory take on the situation,” speculating that Huang’s removal is a way to “remove opposition to an extremely hawkish China export control bill,” referring to the Remote Access Security Act (RASA). The bill, which Huang opposed, would extend AI export controls to cloud servers that allow companies in restricted countries to rent access to Nvidia’s AI chips. The Department of Commerce released an interim final rule on Monday in an attempt to address this loophole.

According to recent reports, more than 185,000 people, including Sweeney, Masad, Elon Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke, have signed a “Stand with Jensen” letter, calling for his reinstatement as CEO. The letter similarly calls for a closer look into the circumstances surrounding Huang’s resignation. “We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the center of this controversy was a spy,” the letter says. “Suspicion or association alone is not a sufficient basis for ending Jensen’s leadership. The inquiry must establish the facts, not merely justify an outcome already imposed.”.

All the questions Nvidia should answer on Tuesday — but probably won’t

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia interim CEO and longtime CFO Colette Kress is about to have one of the biggest days of her career on Tuesday when the firm reports its third-quarter results.
  • For the first time, Kress will be running through the numbers and sharing guidance without Nvidia’s charismatic but now-disgraced founder Jensen Huang.
  • Huang was forced to resign last week after he admitted to having an affair with an exec of a customer, Alice Huang, a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, and he was accused of having two more affairs with Nvidia employees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia interim CEO and longtime CFO Colette Kress is about to have one of the biggest days of her career on Tuesday when the firm reports its third-quarter results.

For the first time, Kress will be running through the numbers and sharing guidance without Nvidia’s charismatic but now-disgraced founder Jensen Huang.

Huang was forced to resign last week after he admitted to having an affair with an exec of a customer, Alice Huang, a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, and he was accused of having two more affairs with Nvidia employees.

Now, the company is facing questions about its restricted chips allegedly being smuggled into China, especially by Huang’s mistress’ company. Nvidia promised to conduct an internal investigation. Meanwhile, Huang was commanded to answer questions to Congress in a closed-door joint session with three Republican-led committees. Plus, top Democrats have also vowed to investigate the company.

Given the turmoil Nvidia is in, there are a number of questions that Kress should answer.

Huang’s role now and going forward. Huang ran Nvidia with an iron fist, having some 60 direct reports and his fingers in everything. No one knows the organization better than him.

Recent findings suggest that an internet petition signed by 180,000 and growing is calling for the board to reinstate him. Huang may also have been mounting an attempt to return, Financial Times reported. However, CNBC is reporting, citing unnamed sources, that the company is not in talks to reinstate Huang.

So, we’ll be looking for language from the interim CEO about Huang’s ongoing involvement with the organization, its search for a new CEO, and any talks to bring him back.

China and Singapore. As Huang vehemently argued in favor of easing export restrictions for Nvidia chips to China, Huang stated that he’s seen no evidence that its powerful semiconductors were being diverted from legit buyers to China.

But in October 2025, The New York Times reported that the U.S. was investigating Huang’s mistress’ tech giant, Megaspeed, over allegations it was doing just that. Nvidia at the time vouched to CNBC that Megaspeed was legally using the chips for its cloud. However, Nvidia recently told The Wall Street Journal that it had voluntarily blocked Megaspeed from receiving more chips way back in June 2025.

Last year, Nvidia mentioned that Singapore, the region where Megaspeed is located, was one of its fastest-growing, accounting for 22% of its total revenue for its second quarter of that year. After the investigation into Megaspeed came to light, Nvidia changed how it reported revenue. It now reports based on a tech giant’s headquarters, instead of its shipping address. That completely hid sales to Singapore and Megaspeed’s impact.

It has been revealed that so we’re listening to what Kress notes about the future of sales to the China region and the cloud business in Singapore that was once 20% of sales. We’re especially listening for what she says about Nvidia keeping track of where its restricted chips wind up.

Industry observers note that china sales policy. Huang’s argument was, essentially, that the U.S. can’t stop China from developing advanced AI models, so the West is better off selling them less powerful Nvidia chips and keeping them dependent, he noted on the Dwarkesh Podcast last summer. Notably, that’s a position that would make Nvidia a lot of money.

Industry observers note that the China hawks counter that selling an adversary any powerful chips at all will help them, and U.S. companies shouldn’t do that. So we’re listening for any indications that Kress is reversing Nvidia’s goals with China.

Bankrolling the AI build-out. The expectation is that Kress, the CFO who reportedly had unsuccessfully tried to push back against Huang’s extreme AI dealmaking, will be conservative on such deals going forward. We’ll be listening for what she claims about the impacts of existing deals on the books. (Will she subtly try to throw Huang under the bus for those controversial deals?) We’ll also be listening for her future aims.

Governance. With the ousting of Huang and more fallout sure still to come, has the board learned its lesson about too much power in the hands of one person? We’ll be listening for information about how Nvidia might restructure itself.

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • October has rolled around, and that means only one thing: Spooky season is here!
  • We’re bringing you a more retro-tinged selection of the best films on streaming this month, but the mix of crowd-pleasers and cult classics offers something for horror fans of all tastes.
  • It has been revealed that if you fancy something a bit newer, fear not.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

October has rolled around, and that means only one thing: Spooky season is here! And what better way to celebrate Halloween than with some of the finest fright fests of the last 50 years?

We’re bringing you a more retro-tinged selection of the best films on streaming this month, but the mix of crowd-pleasers and cult classics offers something for horror fans of all tastes. For instance, David Cronenberg’s grotesque revamp of The Fly, buzzing onto Hulu, and Ken Russell’s Altered States materializing on The Criterion Channel, both bring uniquely visceral takes on body horror to your screens, while sleeper hit Under the Skin on Netflix offers slow-burn sci-fi scares, and Midsommar on Prime Video takes to the hills for a sun-drenched approach to folk horror.

It has been revealed that if you fancy something a bit newer, fear not. Well, fear lots actually—Zach Cregger’s shockingly original horror debut Barbarian smashes its way onto Hulu, while Netflix brings the final chapter in the sumptuously scary Mononoke trilogy, an anime extravaganza that looks like nothing else. Plus, there’s even one post-credits stinger of an entry that’s too scary to mention here ….

Here are WIRED’s picks of the best movies to watch right now.

When Tess (Georgina Campbell) finds her Airbnb in a sketchy neighborhood double booked with Keith (Bill Skarsgård), you’ll probably think you know where Barbarian is headed. You don't—and you should brace yourself for everything that follows. Written and directed by Zach Cregger (in a seismic departure from his early comedy background), Barbarian constantly flips the script, regularly subverting viewer expectations of horror movie clichés at every turn.

Smartly written, brilliantly shot, and psychologically disturbing on multiple levels, Barbarian is a genuinely terrifying entry in the modern horror canon. If you’ve discovered Cregger’s work from the Academy Award–winning Weapons or his recent horror-comedy reboot of Resident Evil, this is where he first made his mark on the silver screen.

Under the Skin almost defies explanation. Scarlett Johansson plays an alien in human form, roaming Glasgow and the Scottish Highlands, luring isolated and lonely men to their doom, drowning them in an inexplicable oily abyss that seems to exist in a null space. All the while, she’s observed by a motorcyclist, trailing her from victim to victim.

Recent findings suggest that no names are given, no purpose explained (not even to the cast; director Jonathan Glazer shot many of the alien’s initial encounters with humans using hidden cameras, only explaining and asking for their involvement afterward), but it’s far better to watch this blind and make your own mind up. Be warned, though—Johansson’s performance is truly unearthly, and in conjunction with Glazer’s bizarre imagery and a soundscape that maddeningly claws at your nerves, this is a deeply unsettling slice of sci-fi.

This acclaimed indie horror movie stars Florence Pugh as Dani, an American student struggling to deal with a family tragedy, who joins her boyfriend Christian (Jack Reynor) and his friends on a trip to Sweden. The vacation sounds like the perfect escape—nine days of communing with nature at a festival held only once every 90 years; a true once-in-a-lifetime experience. The problem? The festival is a front for a pagan cult, and things get rapidly, wildly out of hand.

Midsommar is a deeply effective and distressing folk horror film, with none other than Jordan Peele, director of the smash hit Get Out, declaring it has "the most atrociously disturbing imagery I've ever seen on film." Perfect date night material for Halloween season, then.

Industry observers note that south Korean cinema seems to love combining the end of the world and trains. Bong Joon Ho’s Snowpiercer got things on track in 2013, but director Yeon Sang-ho really left the station with this 2016 zombie horror masterpiece.

Seok-woo (Gong Yoo) starts his journey on the express train from Seoul to Busan just wanting to drop daughter Su-an off with her mother. Unfortunately, the last passenger to board might be a teensy bit infected with the zombie plague that’s kicking off outside, turning the ride into the express train to hell. The tight confines allow for some incredibly inventive action choreography, while genre fans are treated to a revolting twist on the undead themselves, a misshapen, juddering, ravenous horde that moves like a liquid mass of corpses.

It has been revealed that like all the best zombie films, though, it’s the social commentary that really elevates Train to Busan, with its exploration of class and status standing alongside Romero’s work at his peak. A decade on from release, this is still one of the freshest takes on zombies you’re likely to find—look up animated prequel Seoul Station and stand-alone sequel Peninsula if it leaves you wanting another bite.

A bit of a deep cut, but director Ken Russell’s 1980 outing will really mess with your head. No, really—this tale of psychological horror and transformational terror is loosely based on real-world tests of the effects of psychoactive drugs and sensory deprivation on the human brain. The film sees researcher Eddie Jessup (William Hurt) subjecting himself to highly questionable experiments with hallucinogenics and isolation in an effort to tap into other states of being. Unfortunately, he’s wildly successful, not only opening his mind to genetic memories and shared consciousnesses, but seeing his physical body horrifyingly warp and devolve beyond recognition with each trip.

Sources indicate that and what a trip—Russell masterfully creates a sense of psychedelic overload with a pioneering use of bizarre imagery and sound, the film shifting with each of Jessup’s transformations until you feel you’ve taken mind-altering substances yourself. An uncomfortably weird experience, Altered States will stay on your mind long after the credits roll.

Sources indicate that anne Hathaway is literally a monster—at least she is in this darkly comedic crossover between kaiju flick and character study. After her life in Fresh York falls apart, Gloria (Hathaway) moves back home to New Hampshire. At the same time, a giant monster starts rampaging across Seoul, destroying buildings and causing mass panic. Yet these two incompatible events aren't unrelated, as Gloria starts to realize that she can somehow control the beast from half a world away—but her heavy drinking and constant bad decisions may get in the way of saving the world. Director Nacho Vigalondo lovingly pastiches the likes of Godzilla, Gamera, and King Kong in this quirky film festival favorite.

A nameless Medicine Seller (Hiroshi Kamiya in Japanese, Crispin Freeman in English) traveling Edo period Japan may seem a humble figure, but his strange tinctures and concoctions make him one of the few capable of tackling mononoke—powerful spirits corrupting places and people alike. This trilogy-capping third movie takes the enigmatic traveler back to the cursed Imperial Palace visited in predecessors Phantom in the Rain and Ashes of Rage, seeking to uncover once and for all why it seems to attract so many dangerous monsters.

According to recent reports, A master class in tension and otherworldly horror, Mononoke maintains its stunning visual approach of kaleidoscopic watercolors swirling on parchment, making for one of the most sumptuous and visually striking pieces of animation you’ll ever see. It’s worth noting that there is some real-world controversy over a returning voice actor embroiled in a scandal in Japan, so this might be a rare case where the English dub is the better option.

Despite being a remake, David Cronenberg’s quintessential slice of 1980s body horror has almost completely supplanted the 1958 original in the public consciousness (although the original stars Vincent Price and is definitely still worth checking out on Prime Video).

Industry observers note that this wholesale reimagining twists expectations away from mad science clichés—it almost feels like a superhero origin movie to start, with scientist Seth Brundle (Jeff Goldblum) accidentally splicing his genes with a fly during a teleportation experiment, and emerging with enhanced physical prowess in every respect. But with great power comes great personality shifts, wiry black hairs growing along his back, and the need to vomit acid onto his food before eating. And, as animal instincts take over, the self-proclaimed “Brundlefly” starts looking at science reporter Ronnie Quaife (Geena Davis) very differently.

The groundbreaking effects work that marked Brundle’s slow metamorphosis into a repulsive hybrid monster won the film the Oscar for Best Makeup, but its ability to pack in some genuine emotion alongside the scares make it easy to see why this is the de facto iteration of The Fly.

Oh, you think this isn’t horror? Ask yourself: What could possibly be scarier than the deleterious impact social media has had on the human condition? Director David Fincher and writer Aaron Sorkin’s biopic telling of the rise, and rise, and rise of Facebook, is the kind of film you watch through your fingers, too.

There’s an almost predatory hunger in Jesse Eisenberg’s Mark Zuckerberg, as he goes from a Harvard student whose hotness-ranking website was popular enough to crash the college’s whole network to a Silicon Valley darling attracting unheard-of sums of investment and power. Like most “based on a true story” horror films, it’s not entirely historically accurate and, true to genre norms, there’s a not-as-good sequel, with Sorkin returning to write and direct the newly released The Social Reckoning, but if you’ve been paying attention to reality the past few decades, this will definitely chill you to the bone.

Tech Report: How to put your iPad in recovery mode (with and without a home button)

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (555 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A failed update or a forgotten passcode doesn't have to mean the end of your iPad.
  • According to recent reports, many iPad problems can be fixed with a simple restart, but sometimes that's not enough.
  • Recovery mode also lets you connect your iPad to your computer to patch it, or in the worst-case scenario, restore it to its factory default settings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A failed update or a forgotten passcode doesn't have to mean the end of your iPad.

According to recent reports, many iPad problems can be fixed with a simple restart, but sometimes that's not enough. Severe challenges with the tablet's software can make it completely inoperable, and in these cases, putting the iPad in recovery mode might be your only option.

Recovery mode also lets you connect your iPad to your computer to patch it, or in the worst-case scenario, restore it to its factory default settings. It's best to save recovery mode for when nothing else works, but when it's needed, it can mean the difference between a bricked iPad and one that works just like new.

Industry observers note that there are a few situations when you might want to use recovery mode. Major software updates can sometimes fail, leaving you with a partially installed upgrade that keeps your iPad from turning on. Your iPad might reboot itself continuously, or you might enter the wrong passcode too many times and get locked out. Your computer might also stop recognizing your iPad, or your iPad might show a screen prompting you to connect it to a computer.

Recent findings suggest that to put your iPad in recovery mode, first connect it to your computer with a USB cable, and open Finder on Mac or the Apple Devices app on PC. From here, the process differs based on whether your iPad has a home button or not. If it does, hold the home and the power button down at the same time. Eventually, your iPad screen will go black and then show the Apple logo. Finally, it will show the recovery mode icon: an image of a USB cable connecting to a computer. Now release the buttons.

According to recent reports, newer iPads, like the iPad Pro, don't have a home button, so you need to use the power and volume buttons instead. First press and release the volume up button and then the volume down button. Next, press and hold the power button, and keep holding it through the Apple logo until the recovery mode icon appears. Then let go.

Sources indicate that at this point, you can use the Finder or Apple Devices on your computer to find your iPad. If the process worked, you should see a pop-up explaining that the iPad needs to be restored or updated. It's best to start with the enhancement option, which will allow your computer to reinstall iPadOS without affecting anything else stored on your device.

Recent findings suggest that if this option is successful, you'll be able to use your iPad again without losing any data. If it doesn't work, though, you'll have to put it back in recovery mode and choose the restore option. This will restore the iPad to its factory settings, completely erasing your data in the process.

Industry observers note that you can restore everything from your most recent backup (if you have enough iCloud storage), but it's a far more disruptive process that should only be used as a last resort. If your iPad still isn't working after trying both options or you can't get it to enter recovery mode, it may be time to get it professionally repaired or shop for a newly introduced iPad.

#660. Did a Single Router Ground the Nation’s Flights? Experts Express Doubt

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1054 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cnet ↗ Open Full Page

Did a Single Router Ground the Nation’s Flights? Experts Express Doubt

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1054 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The humble internet router is at the center of another national firestorm.
  • Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy stated Sunday that a single router in Arkansas was to blame for the nearly 5-hour-long ground stop on Friday.
  • FAA investigators zeroed in on a routine network upgrade at a radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, where a copper wire line was being upgraded to fiber optic cable by the contractor L3Harris.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The humble internet router is at the center of another national firestorm.

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy stated Sunday that a single router in Arkansas was to blame for the nearly 5-hour-long ground stop on Friday. It was only the second nationwide halt to US air travel since Sept. 11, 2001, leading to the cancellation of 12,462 flights on Friday alone.

FAA investigators zeroed in on a routine network upgrade at a radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, where a copper wire line was being upgraded to fiber optic cable by the contractor L3Harris. A fresh router that came online during the upgrade may have overwhelmed the older equipment, investigators say.

“Either through contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment, that router that was being replaced as we switched from copper to fiber, it started flooding other routers in our air traffic control system,” Duffy said in an interview Sunday.

According to recent reports, this sent a barrage of data through the FAA’s internal communication system — about 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds – that air traffic controllers use to help guide pilots through the country’s airspace. When that newly introduced router was turned on, agency officials noticed the same challenges at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, which had undergone similar work weeks before, Duffy mentioned. The routers at the Arkansas and Texas facilities led to 17 out of the FAA’s 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers experiencing network instability, according to the agency.

But some aviation experts say this official explanation strains credulity.

“I don’t think it’s plausible,” Robert W. Mann Jr., the founder of airline analysis and consulting firm R.W. Mann & Company, told CNET. “Given the network architecture, which is fully duplicative and has fallback capabilities on every link and every piece of physical hardware, it’s not credible that one or even two routers would be an issue.”.

The impacts of the nationwide ground stop are reverberating on the other side of the weekend. As of 3:30 p.m. EST, 333 flights within, into or out of the US have been canceled Monday, according to flight tracking website FlightAware, and more than 3,800 have been delayed.

Industry observers note that the FAA router that grounded tens of thousands of flights looks a lot different from the one that sits in your home. These industrial-grade devices, called switches, are much larger than home Wi-Fi routers and built to withstand harsh conditions. While the agency pointed to the single router in Arkansas as the cause of Friday’s concerns, it says it disabled 60 similar units as a precaution.

FAA Administrator Brian Bedford stated Saturday that the agency is in the process of replacing around 2,000 Cisco routers with 600 Juniper routers. Could any one of those routine equipment upgrades suddenly overload the FAA’s communications system?

According to recent reports, “What surprised me most is the redundancy part for this type of national infrastructure,” Ilia Rabinovich, vice president at the cybersecurity firm Sygnia, told CNET. “This is one of the first things we discuss with clients in terms of preparedness – having backups, having redundancy connectivity, having different connections that you can migrate to different places.”.

Mann thought the timing and symptoms pointed to a fresh $875 million AI-supported air traffic management tool called Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes, and Trajectories, or SMART.

It has been revealed that “What they did starting in September at Baltimore-Washington is at a very low level, for about 60 days. It had managed about 180 flights in total over 60 days,” Mann mentioned. “And then suddenly in November, they confirmed they would implement that system across all 22 continental US air traffic control centers.”.

“You went from subscale to superscale based upon 60 days of very, very limited testing, and within two days, you had the meltdown that they should have known was likely to occur,” Mann stated.

Recent findings suggest that on Oct. 13, more than 25 lawmakers sent a letter to the FAA asking it to pause the rollout of the tool, citing a lack of transparency and training for air traffic controllers.

“We have heard from several sources that frontline aviation safety workers were notified of the SMART tool rollout mere days in advance or not at all, giving them no time to learn how the system works, how it is incorporated into their workflow, and what oversight and accountability mechanisms maintain aviation safety standards,” the letter claims.

According to recent reports, the FAA says in an FAQ page on the incident that the SMART system wasn’t responsible for the issue. A representative for the agency didn’t immediately respond to CNET’s request for comment.

The FAA’s acting CTO, Rebecca Guy, noted at a press conference Saturday that the FAA identified the routers in Arkansas and Texas and disabled “both of those right away and were able to stabilize our network.” But the Transportation Secretary’s interviews over the weekend didn’t instill a lot of confidence in the FAA network’s resilience.

Recent findings suggest that “We have old switches, old routers. We use 1980s little copper lines. It’s an old system that went down and went down everywhere. It got overloaded,” Duffy said at a Friday night news conference.

Industry observers note that the FAA has upgraded over 3,500 of its communication lines to fiber, but more than 5,000 copper lines are still scheduled to be replaced by the end of 2028. It’s eye-opening to see how reliant the FAA still is on copper lines, a technology that the Federal Communications Commission has for years deemed insufficient for average home internet customers.

It didn’t take long for officials to point to funding as the ultimate cause of Friday’s groundings. Duffy repeatedly called for more funding over the weekend in order to upgrade the outdated system.

Recent findings suggest that “The government and FAA are looked on as the piñata here because every time you beat on FAA or beat on the government for not doing a good job, money falls out,” Mann stated. “It didn’t take, what, 6 hours, before we had a cabinet secretary basically saying if we gave him $50 billion, he would fix all this.”.

Duffy had asked for $30 billion for the FAA in September. After Friday’s fiasco, he increased his request by $20 billion.

Breaking: Microsoft blames its Microsoft 365 outage on a dormant July revision defect

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (727 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that microsoft has traced last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage to a July patch for its network gateway servers.
  • Microsoft published the report to customers in the Microsoft 365 admin centre on 15 November, The Register reported.
  • “A latent defect caused servers to become overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions,” Lamanna wrote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that microsoft has traced last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage to a July patch for its network gateway servers. The bug lay dormant for more than three months before a surge in load and a drop in capacity set it off, according to the company’s preliminary post-incident report.

Microsoft published the report to customers in the Microsoft 365 admin centre on 15 November, The Register reported. Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president for Copilot, agents and platform, posted an abridged version on X on Monday, ZDNET reported.

“A latent defect caused servers to become overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions,” Lamanna wrote.

The July revision was built specifically for the Microsoft 365 network gateway servers. It passed load testing and ran worldwide without problems, Microsoft said. But the defect caused lock contention inside an internal Windows process, which exhausted a server’s CPU and memory.

Testing missed it, because the load tests focused on weaker hardware with fewer cores, according to the report. The contention is worse on newer machines with more cores.

Two other conditions then met. Teams failed over to the gateway that also carries Exchange Online, which raised the load. At the same time, an unrelated issue from the day before had taken nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity out of service.

Recent findings suggest that when a server stopped responding, traffic moved to the next healthy one, which then hit the same bug. Within two hours, more than 80% of the servers were unresponsive at the lowest point, the report states.

In a recent development, waiting traffic overwhelmed servers again as soon as they came back online. Microsoft said its automated recovery was not designed for such a broad failure.

“Since the main code defect was a latent bug from several months previous, our normal rollback, flighting, and feature flags were unable to swiftly revert the change,” Lamanna wrote.

According to recent reports, engineers instead wrote an upgrade that returned the Windows code path to its previous state. They applied it to groups of servers in turn. Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint, and the Office apps could move off the faulty gateways and came back sooner. Exchange Online could not, for scale reasons, which is why Outlook was down longest.

The report’s timeline, as published by The Register, starts with the Teams failover at 01:07 UTC on 12 November. The first support case came in at 16:33 UTC. Microsoft applied its fix from 07:20 UTC on 13 November and sent its final customer upgrade at 04:15 UTC on 14 November.

More than 1,000 engineers and other staff joined outage calls led by Lamanna and cloud chief Scott Guthrie, Bloomberg reported. On 13 November, Microsoft apologised and remarked the cause was not a cyberattack or AI agents.

We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services.

This was a technical concern not related to cyber or AI / agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions.

Industry observers note that given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage. While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration.

We will provide a full post-incident report once our review is complete.

— Microsoft (@Microsoft) November 13, 2026.

The outage hit governments, courts, hospitals, and businesses. Downdetector logged reports from 74 countries and territories, according to the Associated Press. TNW covered the restoration of services and Europe’s sovereignty debate that followed.

Last month, a Google Cloud outage in its London region hit services including Revolut.

House Homeland Security Committee chair Andrew Garbarino told Politico he was seeking more information from Microsoft and CISA.

“We need to understand what happened and how to make these systems more resilient,” Garbarino remarked.

Microsoft plans to publish its final post-incident report on 20 November, according to The Register.

Robo-soldier startup backed by Eric Trump misses payroll, may collapse

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A humanoid robotics organization backed and advised by President Donald Trump’s son, Eric Trump, has reportedly missed payroll and may be on the brink of collapse after a funding shortfall.
  • It has been revealed that foundation failed to pay employees for the payroll period ending on October 30, anonymous sources told CNBC.
  • This comes as Pathak and Foundation’s leadership are still looking to raise funding to support a $3 billion valuation, based on their promise to develop a humanoid robot ready for combat duty and capable of wielding various weapons.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A humanoid robotics organization backed and advised by President Donald Trump’s son, Eric Trump, has reportedly missed payroll and may be on the brink of collapse after a funding shortfall. The Silicon Valley startup, Foundation Future Industries, claims it is developing and testing robots for military roles on battlefields from Ukraine to Gaza.

It has been revealed that foundation failed to pay employees for the payroll period ending on October 30, anonymous sources told CNBC. The startup’s staff is especially angry because Foundation’s co-founder and CEO, Sankaet Pathak, supposedly borrowed $4.6 million in company funds to buy a luxury home overlooking San Francisco Bay about a year ago.

This comes as Pathak and Foundation’s leadership are still looking to raise funding to support a $3 billion valuation, based on their promise to develop a humanoid robot ready for combat duty and capable of wielding various weapons.

In a recent development, the company has demonstrated a humanoid robot named the Phantom MK-1 and is touting an upcoming robot called the Phantom MK-2. Foundation has touted its humanoid robots for roles in warehouses and other workplaces—but has courted media coverage by claiming it is developing humanoid robots for battlefield use.

Now CNBC’s reporting based on “people with direct knowledge of the matter” indicates that insiders worry the startup could soon collapse without additional funding.

Recent findings suggest that eric Trump holds an equity stake in Foundation and was revealed as its chief strategy advisor in March 2026, according to the Financial Times. Investment funds linked to both Eric Trump and Donald Trump Jr. are involved with multiple military technology companies that have received Pentagon loans and contracts worth more than $3.2 billion as of July 2026, according to The Washington Post.

After Trump claimed that Foundation had “just secured a $24 million contract with the Pentagon” during the Fox Business interview in April, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) responded by questioning whether the Pentagon is “just a cash machine from Trump’s kids now” in a social media post. “This looks like corruption in plain sight,” Warren wrote.

In a recent development, but publicly available evidence does not back up Trump’s claim about Foundation directly receiving US government funding. Federal spending records show that Foundation holds no publicly listed contracts, according to The San Francisco Standard.

Instead, the firm Boardwalk Robotics received four contracts worth $3.22 million prior to being acquired by Foundation in late 2024.

Meanwhile, the Institute for Human & Machine Cognition—a Florida-based nonprofit research institute and research partner to Boardwalk Robotics—secured a $24.8 million Navy contract in 2025, The San Francisco Standard reported.

Industry observers note that this was not the first time that Foundation’s leadership and investors have made unsupported statements. In 2024, General Motors pushed back on Foundation’s claims that it was about to get an investment from the Detroit automaker, according to CNBC.

On November 11, 2026, Mike LeBlanc, co-founder and president of Foundation Future Industries, told the Financial Times that the manufacturer was in talks with the Israeli military to provide humanoid robots for patrol and combat duties in Hamas tunnels beneath Gaza. He also described taking the company’s Phantom MK1 humanoid robot along to tour some of the tunnels.

However, the Israeli defense ministry declined to comment when the Financial Times reached out.

LeBlanc also previously claimed that two of the company’s Phantom MK-1 units went to Ukraine for testing in frontline reconnaissance and logistics roles in February 2026.

But Craig Smith, an independent journalist and host of the podcast Eye on AI, described tagging along during the delivery of the Phantom robots to Ukraine. He remarked that the robots never made it to Ukraine because they were stopped at the border with Poland.

According to recent reports, when questioned by Smith, LeBlanc only said that Foundation had conducted a pilot demonstration at an undisclosed location, without clarifying whether the robots ever reached Ukraine. LeBlanc also walked back a claim that Foundation had demonstrated its humanoid robots to the Ukrainian government organization Brave1.

It has been revealed that promotional videos showing Foundation’s humanoids have not provided evidence that the robots are ready for battlefield deployments. For example, a “mortar demo” video on the manufacturer website dated to May 2026 shows a person handing a mortar shell to one of the humanoid robots, which slowly lowers the shell over the muzzle of a mortar weapon before finally dropping it in.

Industry observers note that whatever happens to Foundation, humanoid robots remain largely unproven technology and have yet to fulfill organization promises that they can become general-purpose robots handling many different tasks. Companies have just begun testing and deploying such robots in greater numbers within relatively controlled environments such as factories and warehouses.

Industry observers note that similarly, humanoid robots have not yet had any impact on the battlefield. Instead, pioneers in robotics warfare such as the Ukrainian military have focused on developing and deploying unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs)—robotic vehicles that roll along on wheels or tank-style caterpillar tracks.

While defending against the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the Ukrainian military has increasingly deployed more ground robots along with swarms of flying drones to make up for a shortfall in human soldiers compared to Russia. Such ground robots have typically been tasked with performing risky supply runs or evacuating wounded soldiers from frontline positions, but have also entered combat while wielding projectile weapons or even explosives when equipped as roving bombs.

Most recently, Ukraine has deployed armed ground robots directly into combat through both amphibious landings and through airdrops. In 2026, part of Ukraine’s counteroffensive success in rolling back Russian territorial gains has included dropping military robots from drones in airborne assaults behind Russian frontline positions.

Whether it's Black Friday or a CEO scandal, NVIDIA GPUs just don't get deep discounts

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you're hoping for a cheap RTX card this November, the memory market has other plans.
  • Industry observers note that jensen Huang threw in the towel on November 12, resigning as NVIDIA's CEO after founding the tech giant more than three decades ago.
  • According to recent reports, with Black Friday less than two weeks away, people want to know whether they can get their mitts on some cheap NVIDIA.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you're hoping for a cheap RTX card this November, the memory market has other plans.

Industry observers note that jensen Huang threw in the towel on November 12, resigning as NVIDIA's CEO after founding the tech giant more than three decades ago. NVIDIA's market value subsequently fell below $4 trillion for the first time since July 2025 before the week was out, leaving the market in a state of flux.

According to recent reports, with Black Friday less than two weeks away, people want to know whether they can get their mitts on some cheap NVIDIA. While some mean the stock, which closed at around $162 on Friday, others mean the RTX 5080 they've had their eyes on all year. Spoiler alert: only one price has fallen, and it'll take more than a CEO scandal to move the needle on the other.

NVIDIA's graphics cards were already selling way beyond their list prices before Huang's scandal began, because AI data centers have spent the year swallowing the memory those cards need. The RTX 5080, for example, debuted at $999 and now starts at $1,999. The RTX 5090 was $1,999 at launch and sells at close to $7,000 at the lower end. Black Friday has a long record of barely denting GPU prices, and this year retailers have even less room than usual.

Sources indicate that NVIDIA's stock had already dropped by around 20 percent over five straight weeks of losses before its board opened an investigation into Huang on November 8. That included a 9 percent drop following the midterm results and ballot measures that could slow data center construction.

Industry observers note that reports in late October then linked Jensen Huang to Alice Huang, a Singapore-based exec whom U.S. officials reportedly suspect of spying for China. He then admitted to an affair with Alice Huang on November 8. Four days later, Jensen Huang was out as NVIDIA CEO, and by Friday's close the tech giant had posted six consecutive weekly losses. That's its longest streak since 2012, with roughly $1.7 trillion in market value shed since early October.

Industry observers note that HSBC downgraded NVIDIA from buy to hold on November 13, cutting its price target from $365 to $170, arguing that the stock would languish until the company names a permanent CEO. Colette Kress is acting as interim CEO in the meantime while continuing as CFO, a role she has held since 2013. Shares fell another 3.7 percent in premarket trading on Monday, a day before what will be NVIDIA's first-ever earnings report without Jensen Huang.

Sources indicate that data centers brought in the lion's share of NVIDIA's $96.2 billion in last-quarter revenue, accounting for $89 billion. That leaves $7.2 billion for everything else, gamers included. The cause is that memory makers have been focusing on AI chips, pushing up the price of GDDR7 memory that RTX 50-series cards need.

Industry observers note that during the crypto-era shortage of 2021, Ethereum miners were snapping up cards that'd otherwise have gone to gamers, causing prices to balloon. That Black Friday, the best GPU deals were 5 to 10 percent off prices that were themselves already way too high. A year later, the miners were gone. Crypto prices crashed in May 2022, and Ethereum's switch to proof-of-stake that September instantly wiped out GPU mining profitability on the network, yet retailers still sold the RTX 3080 at its $699 list price while calling it a Black Friday deal.

Even without miners competing for stock, Tom's Hardware saw no real GPU deals over the 2023 Black Friday weekend, and in 2024 RTX 4090s were selling above $2,000 against their $1,599 MSRP. By the run-up to last year's Black Friday event, some RTX 50-series cards had settled within $30 of their list prices, but the sales barely had an impact. A PNY RTX 5060 down $20 to $279 made Windows Central's list of NVIDIA deals, while the cheapest RTX 5090 PC Gamer could find was $2,700, $700 over the list price. Those were the best conditions for any potential GPU deals in five years, and they led to discounts measured in tens of dollars.

Industry observers note that retailers heading into Black Friday on November 27 are holding RTX 50-series stock bought at wholesale prices that NVIDIA's Chinese board partners raised again in November. Yes, a Black Friday sale could shave some margin off the top, but any deals will still only be a very modest cut at best from record GPU prices. NVIDIA's stock price, meanwhile, will keep reacting to the likes of earnings and the board's choice of successor. Its GPUs, however, answer to the memory market and the data centers buying up all the organization's output.

#653. Industry News: The vital Gmail security settings you should be using

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (808 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: The vital Gmail security settings you should be using

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (808 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Having your Google account compromised can be a huge deal.
  • It has been revealed that google is very aware of that, which is why it offers a variety of security and privacy settings to keep your account safe and keep third parties out of it.
  • In a recent development, start with Security Checkup; it's a page in your Google Account that gives you personalized recommendations, like adding a recovery phone number and email.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Having your Google account compromised can be a huge deal.

It has been revealed that google is very aware of that, which is why it offers a variety of security and privacy settings to keep your account safe and keep third parties out of it. These are some of the most vital ones you should be using.

In a recent development, start with Security Checkup; it's a page in your Google Account that gives you personalized recommendations, like adding a recovery phone number and email. Those might sound like very basic steps, but they matter more than you might think: Google uses them to alert you to suspicious activity and to help you get back in if someone locks you out. From google.com, click your profile icon in the upper right, then click Manage your Google Account. Click Security & sign-in. At the top of the page, you'll see an icon. A green shield means nothing needs your attention right now. A blue, yellow or red exclamation mark means there's something to fix.

Recent findings suggest that the single biggest fix is two-step verification, also known as two-factor authentication. With it on, a stolen password isn't enough, because signing in also takes something you physically have on you, like your phone or your own computer. To switch it on, go to Security & sign-in, find the How you sign in to Google section, select Turn on 2-Step Verification and follow the prompts.

Then there are passkeys, which let you sign in with your fingerprint, face scan or screen lock instead of a password. A passkey can't be shared, copied or written down, so it holds up against phishing. To create one, go to your account's passkey page and select Create a passkey. Only do it on devices you own; once a passkey exists, anyone who can unlock that device can get into your account.

Locking the front door doesn't help if someone already has a key, so check who and what is connected. Go to myaccount.google.com, open Security & sign-in and scroll down to the linked apps section, then select See all linked apps. You'll see the apps and sites you use Sign in with Google for, plus anything that has been given access to your account data. Anything you don't recognize or no longer use can go: select Remove access, then Confirm.

Next, look at Gmail itself. An attacker who gets in often changes a few quiet settings so they can keep reading your mail later. Open Gmail on your computer, click the gear icon in the top right and select See all settings. Then check for anything unfamiliar under automatic forwarding, filters, labels, scheduled emails, your vacation responder, and IMAP or POP access. Mail delegation, which lets someone else read, send and delete email in your account, has its own spot: go to the Accounts and Import tab and look under Grant access to your account. If a name is there that you didn't add, click Delete next to it. You can't manage delegates from the Gmail app, only on the desktop site. Automatic forwarding is the nasty one. It sends a copy of every new message, except spam, to another address, and you'd never notice. If you find a forwarding rule you didn't set up, change your password right away and turn it off.

Industry observers note that the devices page is the other place to look. It lives in your Google Account, not in Gmail's settings: go to myaccount.google.com, open Security & sign-in (on a computer it may show up as just Security in the left-hand menu), find Your devices and select Manage all devices. You'll see everywhere you're signed in or have been in the last few weeks. Watch for a device you don't recognize, a location you weren't in or a browser you don't normally use. Take a moment to think about it, though: an airport, a library computer or a phone you recently reset can all look odd. If something really isn't yours, select the device and tap Sign out.

It has been revealed that once the settings are in place, a few habits keep them working. Keep two-step verification on, and never share a verification code with anyone. Google guarantees it won't call you to ask for one. Run Security Checkup again every now and then, since recommendations change and old devices and apps pile up.

Sources indicate that in general, keep an eye out for any suspicious activity, or even lack of activity. For example, you stop receiving mail, friends tell you they got spam from you, there are emails sent that you didn't write or messages vanish from your inbox without landing in Trash. If any of that sounds familiar, change your password first, then work through the devices, apps and Gmail settings above.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cybersecurity and automation giant Infoblox has confirmed a cybersecurity incident, during which hackers accessed company information through one of its technology vendors.

Infoblox is a privately held cyber giant that provides companies cybersecurity and networking services, such as domain name resolution and identity and user access management.

In a statement, a spokesperson for Infoblox told TechCrunch that the company is “investigating a security event involving unauthorized access to certain company information through a compromised third-party data migration vendor.”.

“We immediately activated our incident response procedures, took steps to contain the incident and are working with leading outside cybersecurity experts to investigate the facts, understand the scope and address any confirmed risks.”.

TechCrunch has learned that the data breach involves a vendor that provides SharePoint data migration services, according to a notification sent by Infoblox about the breach, two people with knowledge of the incident told TechCrunch.

One of the people noted sensitive customer data was taken in the breach.

According to recent reports, according to public internet records seen by TechCrunch, Infoblox hosts much of its files, emails, and infrastructure with Microsoft, including a SharePoint server, which TechCrunch confirmed is accessible through Infoblox’s single sign-on provider. SharePoint is web-based software that companies use to share and host internal files and documents.

Infoblox has not named the third-party migration vendor that was hacked, but one person with knowledge of the incident remarked that Infoblox has terminated its work with the vendor.

The company’s spokesperson did not comment on this, but added that the company has “no indication that any Infoblox products, cloud services, software updates or build-and-release processes were involved” in the breach.

In a recent development, infoblox would not say how many customers were affected by the incident, or if the firm is aware at this time. The company also did not say, when asked, if it had been contacted by the hackers and if they had made any demands.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s only available in Turkey and Thailand for now.

Industry observers note that meta is working on a dedicated messaging app for Instagram that could also expand the reach of the app's DMs. The company is starting to test Direct, a latest standalone app that brings Instagram's inbox to a separate app, but doesn't require an existing Instagram account to use. Direct will only be available in Thailand and Turkey for now, Meta stated in an update.

In a recent development, meta says it's also bringing some of Instagram's safety features to Direct. The app won't allow people to start chats with accounts they aren't already connected with via their contacts. And parents will be able to monitor who their teen is chatting with and how much time they spend in the app if they use the company's parental control features. Additionally, Meta says it will "use technology to detect and act on potentially inappropriate interactions with young people," though it's vague about what exactly that will entail.

According to recent reports, the test of Direct is an interesting move for Meta. Instagram head Adam Mosseri often notes that messaging is Instagram's most-used feature. But he was also reluctant to give Threads its own inbox because it seemed "redundant" to use multiple apps to reach the same people when Meta briefly considered bringing Instagram's inbox to Threads. He stated at the time that mirroring the Instagram inbox could cause "notification routing weirdness" and generally seemed like a less than ideal experience for most people.

Recent findings suggest that the app also raises questions about whether Direct would compete with WhatsApp in the countries where it's rolled out. It's unlikely an Instagram-centric app would replace WhatsApp for many people, but it could eat into that app's engagement if non-Instagram customers can use Direct to message friends instead.

Sources indicate that that may also be why Direct seems fairly limited for now. Meta describes it as a test that will only be available to people in Turkey and Thailand for the time being. But if the app is a success, it's likely the tech giant will consider expanding it to more places.

School Campuses Emerge as the Latest Battleground for Flock Safety Cameras

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (588 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cnet

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the last year, a backlash against surveillance technologies from companies like Flock Safety has caused agencies in communities, including Los Angeles and Dayton, Ohio, to reevaluate or cancel their contracts for tools such as license plate reader cameras and drones.
  • Now, some college and high school campuses are taking the same steps, reconsidering whether the value of identifying potential crime suspects or providing first-responder information is worth the privacy trade-offs.
  • Sources indicate that A recent story in The Guardian points to dozens of schools, mostly college campuses, where contracts with Flock have been discontinued or where student protests and activism are pressuring administrations to cut ties.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the last year, a backlash against surveillance technologies from companies like Flock Safety has caused agencies in communities, including Los Angeles and Dayton, Ohio, to reevaluate or cancel their contracts for tools such as license plate reader cameras and drones.

Now, some college and high school campuses are taking the same steps, reconsidering whether the value of identifying potential crime suspects or providing first-responder information is worth the privacy trade-offs.

Sources indicate that A recent story in The Guardian points to dozens of schools, mostly college campuses, where contracts with Flock have been discontinued or where student protests and activism are pressuring administrations to cut ties. Some of the schools that have walked away from Flock include Cornell University, Emory University, Penn State University and Stanford University, where a coalition called Safe Stanford successfully organized to convince school officials. At Stanford, the university chose to switch from Flock to technology from Genetec, which stores data for only an hour and doesn’t share information with third parties.

Some of the most recent campus protests against using Flock technology have been on the University of Iowa campus, where 2,000 petition signatures were delivered to campus police, and at the University of Kentucky, where student groups chanted, “Flock out! Flock off!”.

Flock, which is one of several companies, including Axon Enterprise, Motorola Solutions and Palantir Technologies, that provide surveillance hardware and software to law enforcement, has been heavily criticized for license plate reader failure rates and abuses within law enforcement.

In an email to CNET, the Atlanta-based company declined to offer the number of colleges or schools it works with, though a recent research paper published in Policing & Society put the number at around 150.

Flock stressed in its email to CNET that customers it contracts with own and control their own data.

“Students deserve to feel safe at school, and Flock license plate reader technology has a measurable impact on helping to solve crimes and increase public safety,” the spokesperson remarked. “Flock LPR cameras capture a point-in-time image of the rear of a vehicle. Flock does not use facial recognition, cannot identify who is inside a vehicle and cannot determine who the vehicle is registered to.”.

When government agencies like police departments or county sheriff’s offices employ a firm like Flock to provide surveillance services, it typically involves installing cameras in public locations and pointing them at street intersections or on buildings.

College and high school campuses may have different rules for on-campus surveillance and for public schools. They might also be bound by state laws that also apply to government agencies.

“Campuses also raise issues ordinary public streets don’t: students often live there, many are minors, and student-privacy laws and school-search rules vary by state, as do limits on how long plate data can be kept and shared,” said Amy Peikoff, an attorney for the Pacific Legal Foundation.

Peikoff stated that most courts have allowed the collection of the types of data Flock Safety collects. However, Peikoff said that problems can arise regarding how long agencies such as police departments or schools can retain the data they collect. In the past, activists have pointed to abuses that have occurred when law enforcement workers inappropriately accessed or shared information collected by Flock, in some cases, using it for stalking.

“Maintaining a vast, queryable database of location histories of individuals about whom there’s no particularized suspicion not only presents an opportunity for abuse, but is in itself, I believe, a Fourth Amendment violation,” Peikoff remarked.

Arion Kurtaj leaked 90 videos of GTA VI years before its release.

Arion Kurtaj, a member of the Lapsus$ cybercrime group who leaked 90 videos of Grand Theft Auto VI in 2022 and hacked other significant companies, pleaded guilty on Monday, according to the UK’s Crown Prosecution Service (CPS).

Kurtaj, who is now 21, hacked BT/EE sometime between August and November 2021, and starting in early November of that year, the company “noted a marked increase in unauthorised SIM swaps of their customers mobile phones.” He was charged for those offenses and moved to a hotel for his “own protection” in September 2022, but “breached his bail conditions to carry out further hacks on major companies using a mobile phone, the hotel TV’s Wi-Fi and a firestick,” including hacks on Rockstar Games, Uber, and Revolut, the CPS states.

He was sentenced to life in a secure hospital in December 2023 because of his autism, but in January, Kurtaj was deemed fit for trial and moved to prison, the BBC reports.

Kurtaj is set to be sentenced on November 23rd. GTA VI will be released on November 19th.

Buying a used phone? Make sure to check the IMEI first

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (533 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A phone's IMEI number can reveal whether the device has sketchy history, what networks it can connect to and more.
  • According to recent reports, smartphones are no exception to soaring tech prices and the pre-owned market has become a necessary respite for many.
  • Industry observers note that buying a pre-owned phone from eBay, Facebook Marketplace or a physical repair shop requires a good deal of prep work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A phone's IMEI number can reveal whether the device has sketchy history, what networks it can connect to and more.

According to recent reports, smartphones are no exception to soaring tech prices and the pre-owned market has become a necessary respite for many. However, whenever you're buying a refurbished or generally pre-owned phone, you need to take a few precautions. In particular, you need to look out for the red flags of a potential scam and every mobile device has a special number that can help you.

Industry observers note that buying a pre-owned phone from eBay, Facebook Marketplace or a physical repair shop requires a good deal of prep work. You should properly clean and sanitize the secondhand phones you find while also making sure the phone you're getting doesn't have any obvious defects. When you're asking the seller about the device's condition and history, you should also ask about the phone's IMEI number — which can reveal whether a phone has sketchy history, what networks it can connect to, and more.

Sources indicate that every mobile device has a unique 15-digit number associated with it known as an International Mobile Equipment Identity (IMEI) number. This number is used to register your phone with your network provider and can subsequently be used by that provider to identify your phone. If your phone is lost or stolen, you can contact your provider and have them blacklist your phone via that IMEI number.

Industry observers note that if you want to find your phone's IMEI number, it can typically be found in the device's packaging or on any physical or digital receipts, as well as on your network provider account. Additionally, while you can generally find your IMEI number in your phone's settings, dialing *#06# into the keypad of any phone will reveal its unique IMEI code. You can also contact your provider's support team about finding this number if all else fails.

According to recent reports, if you're in the position of buying a latest phone, the device's seller should provide its IMEI code to you upon request — and you should definitely ask for this code. The IMEI number will help you confirm whether it's been stolen or whether it's compatible with certain cellular networks.

There are all too many scams to avoid when buying refurbished tech online and in person, so be on the lookout for sellers that refuse to provide the IMEI number as they may be selling fenced goods. An IMEI number can't be used to hack or track phones by itself but sellers should only share it with serious buyers through private messaging and buyers should keep screenshots of the conversation just in case.

In a recent development, upon being provided with an IMEI number, you should proceed with checking its validity and whether it's been reported stolen or lost. There's quite the smorgasbord of sites to use if you want to check an IMEI number, many of which will ask for a small fee before checking the number. While many of the options are free, research whichever site you use first to make sure you're not about to fall for a phishing scam.

Android tablets are back, but are they for you?
