#598. Jensen Huang and the End of the Founder Fairy Tale

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (945 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Jensen Huang and the End of the Founder Fairy Tale

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (945 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, I had agreed to travel to Denver, Colorado, to interview the Nvidia CEO at SIGGRAPH, the annual confab of computer graphics PhDs and practitioners.
  • What ensued was, in a word, bizarre.
  • Industry observers note that slides?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was July of 2024, and Jensen Huang was punchy.

According to recent reports, I had agreed to travel to Denver, Colorado, to interview the Nvidia CEO at SIGGRAPH, the annual confab of computer graphics PhDs and practitioners. Early that year I’d conducted a lengthy sit-down interview with Huang for a WIRED magazine feature, which apparently went well enough—both for WIRED and for Nvidia’s executive communications team—that I had been asked to interview Huang again at this conference. Another opportunity to grill the CEO of the modern world’s most consequential firm? Yes, of course. I began preparing.

What ensued was, in a word, bizarre. During the first prep call for the conference, the type of call-in which PR handlers typically try to coax specific questions out of journalists to prevent an ambush, a youngish, vaguely familiar woman took the lead. This was Madison Huang, Jensen’s daughter. She was clearly intelligent, commanding respect. She told me about the slides Jensen would be presenting on stage at SIGGRAPH and offered suggestions for key moments when I might tee him up to talk about the slides.

Industry observers note that slides? Tee up Jensen? What kind of “interview” was this?

According to recent reports, I raised my concerns with both my editors and Nvidia. We agreed that I would ask the questions I intended to ask him, which included questions about the environmental impact of data centers, and that Huang would also be referring to slides. Let’s just say the interview didn’t go smoothly. (It’s on YouTube.) To this day, former and current Nvidia workers sometimes tell me that I “handled” the whole thing well. Huang was domineering, evaded some of my questions, and, immediately after our session concluded, did an impromptu Q&A session with a much more adoring crowd than me. Then I was guided offstage, and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg hopped on, where he and Huang had a lovey-dovey fireside chat.

Industry observers note that as a longtime journalist I’m used to occasional adversarial interactions; I really don’t lose sleep over them. This was just a CEO being a CEO. Huang later agreed to meet with me again, in December 2024. But that interview in Denver had underscored for me how much Jensen Huang wanted to control the narrative. Not just wanted to; he assumed he would. And to a large extent he did. Until this week.

Narrative has always been a critical part of Huang’s success. He was not just your average electrical engineering nerd who toiled away on something that would eventually find a product-market fit. By Huang’s own telling, he was an immigrant founder, an underdog, a wife guy who chased (and eventually married) his college sweetheart, a scrappy startup guy who dined at Denny’s in the early days. A visionary who worked Sundays and who didn’t sleep well because he always heard the hoof steps of competitors. A parent who brought his kids into the corporate fold. A man who loved Nvidia so much he tattooed an abstract version of the tech giant logo on his arm.

Recent findings suggest that huang built the highest-valued publicly traded tech giant in history. That part’s not just fairy tale. It’s true. Now, it’s starting to read more like a Greek tragedy.

Back in January 2024, when I sat down with him for our first-ever in-person meeting, Huang right off the bat talked about the importance of storytelling. Here’s an excerpt:.

Jensen Huang: Somebody who I really admire, as a leader and a person, is Shantanu Narayen, the CEO of Adobe. He said he always wanted to be a journalist because he loved telling stories.

WIRED: It seems like an vital part of building a business, being able to tell its story effectively.

Yes. Strategy setting is storytelling. Culture building is storytelling.

You’ve stated many times you didn’t sell the idea of Nvidia based on a pitch deck.

That’s right. It was really about telling the story.

According to recent reports, of course, even then, Huang was caught up in the crosshairs of the US–China AI war and at the mercy of regulators, as I wrote at the time. After Donald Trump’s reelection that year, Huang once again deployed his storytelling skills and lobbied the Trump administration to loosen export controls, so he could sell some of his company’s chips to China.

Another crucial part of the Huang lore is that he ran a “flat” organization, with a few dozen top executives reporting to him. (This is sometimes reported as being “60” people; insiders have told me at times it’s closer to 35.) Huang once noted the structure allowed Nvidia “to adapt a lot more rapidly, which we need because our technology is moving so quickly.” Huang was also known to be controlling of all aspects of the business—participating in every significant meeting, seemingly aware of every moving part, and staying in the loop on sourcing, supply chains, and the tech giant’s allocation of chips.

Sources indicate that this is where Huang’s cult of leadership, and his Nvidia storytelling, may have come to a stupidly disappointing final chapter. As one former employee put it, Huang can’t simultaneously have had knowledge of every element of Nvidia’s business and then potentially feign ignorance about where the chips may have fallen, both figuratively and literally. His apparent lapses in judgment have now led him to resign from the very company he coaxed into existence and have shattered the mythos of its ever-prescient founder.

It’s certainly not the narrative ending Huang would have chosen, were he still in control.

Update: The ground stop has been lifted, and domestic flights resumed late Friday.

In an extraordinarily rare move, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) announced that all flights in the U.S. are grounded on Friday afternoon.

The FAA said this nationwide ground stop was "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.".

It has been revealed that U.S. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy posted a confirmation of the outage on his X account, attributing the ground stop order to "a communication matter impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.” Duffy added, “FAA technicians are investigating the issue.".

The FAA has only ordered the grounding of all flights nationwide on two prior occasions. The first was on 9/11, and the second was on Jan. 11, 2023, when all flights were grounded for 90 minutes due to problems with the Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) system. In 2024, the CrowdStrike IT outage led some major airlines to matter a global stoppage.

In a recent development, "The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication concerns impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers," the FAA said in a statement. "All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice," read an air traffic control advisory reported by Axios. Flyers can also check the social media profiles and websites of specific airports for local updates.

Samsung is working on a long overdue redesign for its Galaxy S27 series and, this week, we’re getting a fresh look.

All of that said, adding a bit of controversy to this image is leaker Ice Universe, who indicates “this picture is wrong.”.

It has been revealed that ice points out that the Galaxy S27 Ultra and Pro both do not have a fourth camera lens, which is correct based on recent leaks. That stated, it’s not much of a leap to assume these dummy units are based on an older design, or are confusing a sensor. After all, these are mainly used to test accessories and, this early on, there’s plenty of room for inaccuracy.

Samsung may soon be charging for Galaxy AI, potentially ending the uncertainty surrounding how long its artificial intelligence tools will remain free.

A new leak, courtesy of SammyGuru, reveals an interface for Galaxy AI Premium, a monthly plan that adds more AI capabilities. It appears Samsung is working on it, but existing features will likely be spared from the paywall.

According to the leak, customers will have to pay $4.99 a month or $47.99 annually to get access to the premium package.

The existing tools, including Now Brief, Browsing Assist, Creative Studio, and AI-powered Samsung Keyboard features, are likely to remain free.

Samsung has not yet confirmed pricing, feature lineup, or if the paid subscription is coming soon or when.

According to recent reports, if the proposal goes official, Galaxy owners won’t necessarily lose the AI tools they’ve been using already. But Samsung will have to convince customers that $5 a month is a worthwhile price to pay for its upcoming features.

Samsung’s got a potentially bigger problem than subscription fatigue: some Galaxy owners aren’t sold on its AI tools being worth paying for in the first place. Comments in Reddit’s r/Android community indicate people don’t understand the need for another subscription when services such as Gemini and ChatGPT already provide more capable alternatives. One commenter even noted that some Galaxy S25 Ultra owners aren’t even aware of the AI features their phones have.

Others stated they'd pay if Samsung could deliver a more unified, reliable experience. That puts the pressure on Samsung to prove that Galaxy AI Premium offers something genuinely useful, rather than just putting a price tag on features that many owners rarely touch.

It's stated that the Galaxy S27 series could be the initial supported lineup, but it could come more broadly later.

Sources indicate that for only the third time in U.S. history, the Federal Aviation Administration(FAA) has issued a nationwide ground stop of all flights.

U.S. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy confirmed the ground stop at 4:16 p.m. ET. More than 2,000 flights have already been affected and flights into the U.S. have also been halted.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told the press that today's national stoppage was caused by a "telecommunications outage," not a national security threat.

One day prior, ArsTechnica reported on the FAA's recent roll out of its fresh $875 million AI tool, the Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) system. SMART is a cloud-based platform system designed to help air traffic controllers evaluate and manage national airspace, the FAA explained in a system fact sheet. In an effort to “boost driver awareness” of nearby bicycle riders, Waze will start showing real-time alerts for nearby cyclists to drivers in the area. The feature shows both a location on the map ahead as well as a visible alert on screen.

Waze knows the location of a nearby cyclist through a partnership with Garmin, with “LiveTrack” location sharing from the Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin smartwatches users to share location data with the Google-owned navigation app.

In a recent development, cyclists need to opt-in to the feature to have their location shown, and the alerts drivers see are temporary and anonymous. When cyclists end their ride, Waze alerts also go away.

According to recent reports, this feature is completely opt-in and built with privacy in mind. Drivers only see a temporary alert that a cyclist is nearby — never information about a specific cyclist or route. Plus, alerts automatically turn off the moment a cyclist ends their ride on their Garmin device.

This is rolling out starting today to the Waze apps on both Android and iOS.

The Microsoft Outage Is a Warning for the World

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1343 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A dramatic Microsoft 365 outage impacting widely used services like Outlook, Teams, and Copilot dragged into a second day on Friday after the company failed overnight to resolve an concern that left institutions and individuals around the world without crucial communication tools.
  • “We’re observing sustained improvements in service availability,” Microsoft stated in a statement posted to its status dashboard on Friday morning.
  • Sources indicate that the outages have caused widespread disruption to schools, courts, governments, and law enforcement agencies—plus countless businesses and millions of employees—around the globe, highlighting how many of the world’s most crucial systems rely upon technologies from a small number of tech companies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A dramatic Microsoft 365 outage impacting widely used services like Outlook, Teams, and Copilot dragged into a second day on Friday after the company failed overnight to resolve an concern that left institutions and individuals around the world without crucial communication tools. The services did seem to be on a slow path to recovery by midmorning on Friday.

“We’re observing sustained improvements in service availability,” Microsoft stated in a statement posted to its status dashboard on Friday morning. The company had said on Thursday evening that its initial attempts to fix the problem were “not taking as expected.”.

Sources indicate that the outages have caused widespread disruption to schools, courts, governments, and law enforcement agencies—plus countless businesses and millions of employees—around the globe, highlighting how many of the world’s most crucial systems rely upon technologies from a small number of tech companies. And when they fail, the ramifications can be huge.

Microsoft has not remarked yet what caused the outage but has hinted that it was related to cascading server failures inside multiple data centers around the world that shifted too much load onto remaining operational machines.

Recent findings suggest that “We determined the elevated load isn't driven by an increase in traffic, but by a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure,” the firm wrote in Microsoft 365 Status update on Thursday afternoon. “We’re testing a configuration change to address a problem that's causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable,” the company added a few minutes later.

An additional revision a few minutes after that noted, “We've not identified any recent change correlated with the start of impact; however, our investigation indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component that's responsible for processing server health.”.

Microsoft emphasized repeatedly in statements that there was no indication of the outage being caused by a cyberattack.

“This is absolutely going to go down as one of the major ones, up there with the Facebook outage of October 2021,” indicates Doug Madory, head of internet analysis at monitoring firm Infoblox. “We don't know the root cause yet, but it is interesting to break down the traffic by source data center. The recovery came in fits and starts and varied greatly by source, probably due to Microsoft's efforts to bring the service back online.”.

Recent findings suggest that A prolonged outage of such a critical underlying digital service is not unprecedented, but Microsoft has a special position among cloud providers as an older tech giant that was already ubiquitous in global computing from the PC era. Many organizations integrate Microsoft productivity services at the core of their operations, simply because they have used Windows computers for decades and have longstanding relationships with Microsoft.

According to recent reports, “What makes this particularly significant is the criticality of the services affected, especially email and communication systems relied upon by government and other essential organisations,” claims Swapneel Patnekar, the CEO of Indian web security firm Shreshta IT Technologies. “The impact goes well beyond the inconvenience of a typical service disruption.”.

In a recent development, many observers pointed out on Thursday and Friday that Microsoft has recently shed staff through attrition, layoffs, and buyout offers. The manufacturer’s annual filings say it had 223,000 full-time employees on June 30, down from 228,000 at the same time in 2025. Then in July, the company eliminated 9,000 jobs globally, of which 3,200 were cuts related to an overhaul of its Xbox teams. In October, the company reportedly made buyout offers to 60,000 employees, though apparently this was intended to speed attrition, not cull all of those roles.

According to recent reports, then there’s the AI factor. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella noted in April that as much as 30 percent of the code the tech giant is generating is now written using AI in automated tools.

“Satya's recent comments have a much different look today than they did even a week ago,” indicates Jake Williams, a faculty member at IANS, an intelligence and security consultancy. “I don't think we'll ever be able to say that the staff reductions caused this outage, but you'll never convince me that all the tribal knowledge that walked out the door wouldn't have been invaluable in resolving it.”.

Microsoft did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Reports of widespread disruption from the Microsoft outage started appearing during the working day on Friday in countries in Asia and Australasia, spreading across the world as more people logged on.

Schools, retail stores, courts, and medical organizations across Australia remarked everything from exams to health care appointments were disrupted. “Medical scans have been cancelled due to both myself and the clinic not being able to access referrals via email or fax,” one person told Australian media. Officials in Japan’s government said its own platforms had been disrupted, and staff were using phones and chat tools as they couldn’t access Outlook.

Recent findings suggest that in the UK, multiple police forces have said they are unable to accept online crime reports due to the outages of Microsoft services, though phone lines for emergency and nonemergency reports remained available. Parts of the National Health Service, including doctor surgeries and hospital services, also reported that some services were impacted by the outages. “Those who work in 111 and 999 services are unable to refer patients in the normal way—creating a massive backlog,” the GMB trade union posted on X, referring to nonemergency and emergency health services.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, Deutsche Bahn, the provider of train services across Germany, updated its alerts page saying the email outages “severely restricts the sending of timetables.” Courts, local government agencies, and media organizations in the Netherlands reported concerns with their communications services, according to local press. In France, some health agencies and local governments also reported similar issues. One winemaker in South Africa told the BBC his manufacturer had been brought to a standstill by the outages.

Recent findings suggest that unsurprisingly, these disruptions continued to be echoed across Canada and the US as millions of people have attempted to sign on. Canadian rail service Via Rail posted online that customers may not receive details of their booked trips via email, with with York’s Department of Investigation posting on X that housing evictions planned for Friday had been canceled and Arapahoe County Sheriff’s Office, in Colorado, also posting on X that a lack of email notifications means bond payments being made online were not being processed.

Recent findings suggest that “It's literally named 365. That implies a specific duty,” says longtime security and compliance consultant Davi Ottenheimer. “Can’t sell an empty bottle called ‘Bottle of Water.’”.

During the outage, multiple officials around the world called for countries to rely less on giant tech firms or reevaluate their relationships. “The global Microsoft outage only serves to highlight once again the lack of resilience in the UK’s digital infrastructure, and the dangers that this dependency can pose to our security, economy and public services,” Chi Onwurah, the chair of the UK parliament’s Science and Technology Committee, said in a statement.

Sources indicate that since the start of the second Trump administration—with its chaos, unpredictability, and threats changing the nature of international relationships—countries across Europe and other parts of the world have been starting to change their attitudes and reliance on some US-based big technology firms, such as Google, Microsoft, and Amazon Web Services. Officials in France have been developing local, open source alternatives to Zoom, Teams, and other productivity software, while WIRED has documented dozens of other European efforts to ditch US big tech services.

In a recent development, patnekar, from Indian security firm Shreshta, says that while much tech infrastructure has been provided by centralized services in recent years, email seems particularly challenging to create resiliency. “Ultimately, the lesson isn't necessarily that organisations should stop relying on large technology providers,” Patnekar says. “Rather, they need to identify which services are genuinely mission-critical and ensure they have an independent fallback when those providers become unavailable.”.

  • According to recent reports, several sources told CBS News Friday evening that the ground stop was caused by a communication system reboot.
  • Hours later, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin stated the outage was caused by an outdated air traffic control system coming up against the processing power of newly implemented modern technology.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Trump administration officials and Air Traffic Control (ATC) insiders are shedding light on Friday's nationwide ground stop, which resulted in massive delays for thousands of flights and nearly all domestic travelers.

According to recent reports, several sources told CBS News Friday evening that the ground stop was caused by a communication system reboot. According to multiple insiders with knowledge of the incident, an update to a private communications network used by air traffic controllers forced the system to reboot and impede communications at the nation's 22 regional air traffic control centers, CBS News reported.

Hours later, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin stated the outage was caused by an outdated air traffic control system coming up against the processing power of newly implemented modern technology.

Industry observers note that "Our routers got overloaded by the data," said Duffy. The secretary said the overloaded routers, which he described as "'80s copper lines", caused instability in communications at Terminal Radar Approach Control (TRACON) and Air Route Traffic Control Centers (ARTCCs). Out of an "abundance of caution," the FAA issued the ground stop.

Industry observers note that duffy asserted that only older lines were affected, not newly installed ATC tech. Duffy then called on Congress to provide $50 billion in emergency funding to overhaul the system completely. The ground stop has now been lifted.

In a recent development, as recently as 6 p.m. ET, insiders reported the FAA was still investigating the circumstances behind the communication blackout.

Recent findings suggest that following confirmation of a telecommunications outage, social media users theorized the blackout may have been a consequence of the FAA's newly introduced AI-powered air traffic control system, known as Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories, or SMART. Others suggested the recent Microsoft outage could have been a factor.

It has been revealed that when asked if AI played a role in the ground stop, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told the press that officials couldn't "rule anything out." In comments to the press later that evening, Mullin once again affirmed officials haven't found any indication of a cybersecurity attack but couldn't rule out interference entirely. "There’s nothing completely certain right now. It does not appear that way," Mullin remarked. "The public was never at danger. There was never any lives at risk. There were no flights at risk.".

Air Space Intelligence (ASI), the organization behind SMART, denied speculation that the upcoming AI tool was involved in the ground stop. Microsoft also issued a statement, writing: "We have no indication that the FAA’s nationwide ground stop is related to any Microsoft services.".

The FAA has undertaken an administration-wide modernization project, including phasing out the use of floppy disks for storing weather conditions, airport status updates, equipment problems, and other critical information.

PATCH: Nov. 13, 2026, 5:47 p.m. This story was updated with new information from the Department of Transportation and Department of Homeland Security.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Customers visiting the Apple Support Community tonight were greeted with a message informing them that the platform will permanently shut down on November 20. Here are the details.

If you have ever had a question or ran into a problem with an Apple product, chances are you have come across the Apple Support Community, the company’s official discussion forums where consumers from around the world help each other troubleshoot challenges and share tips.

The platform has a history dating back to at least 1998, when it was known as Apple Tech Exchange. Since then, it was renamed Apple Discussions before relaunching as Apple Support Communities in April 2011, with a redesigned interface, personalized profiles, and a reputation system that rewarded owners for helping others.

Tonight, however, owners who tried to access the platform were greeted with the following message:.

Recent findings suggest that the AppleCare Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept newly introduced posts and is available in a read-only state.

You can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site.

We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products.

Right now, the portal still shows a “Sign in” button, though it leads only to an AppleConnect login page labeled “AC Communities Web – Internal,” suggesting that access is now restricted to Apple employees.

Interestingly, Apple’s message refers to the “AppleCare Support Community,” rather than the “Apple Support Community,” which is how the platform is officially branded.

Sources indicate that these forums were often far up when searching for Apple problems, but I’m not sure I ever found a real answer there. So often the threads went no where or someone would link an unhelpful Apple support page.

Still, the forums are already in read-only mode, with people able to browse existing discussions, search for answers, and interact with posts through the “Me too” and voting buttons, but no longer submit new questions or replies.

At the time of writing, the most recent post was published just 57 minutes earlier, suggesting that Apple only recently disabled newly introduced submissions.

9to5Mac has reached out to Apple for comment and clarification on the scope of the shutdown, and we’ll patch this story if we hear back.

We've already seen several leaks surrounding Samsung's upcoming Galaxy S27 series, which is expected to launch in early 2027. Unlike previous years, Samsung is reportedly planning to introduce four models this time around, including the standard Galaxy S27, Galaxy S27 Plus, Galaxy S27 Pro, and Galaxy S27 Ultra.

The new Pro model is expected to bring several Ultra-level features at a slightly lower price, and now a new report suggests Samsung has pretty high expectations for its two higher-end variants.

According to ET News, Samsung is planning to allocate more than 70% of its total Galaxy S27 production to the Galaxy S27 Pro and Galaxy S27 Ultra. The company is reportedly targeting around 35 million units across the entire lineup, with the Galaxy S27 Ultra alone accounting for approximately 18 million units.

Recent findings suggest that interestingly, Samsung is also reportedly planning to produce 7 to 8 million units of the Galaxy S27 Pro, bringing the combined production of the two premium models to around 25 to 26 million units. This means the standard Galaxy S27 and Galaxy S27 Plus will account for just the remaining 9 to 10 million units.

Industry observers note that for comparison, Samsung reportedly produced around 18 million units of the Galaxy S26 Ultra this year, accounting for roughly 50% of the entire Galaxy S26 series production. While the firm isn't necessarily increasing production of the Ultra model next year, it's expecting the upcoming Galaxy S27 Pro to attract buyers who would otherwise have gone for the standard or Plus models.

For those unfamiliar, the Galaxy S27 Pro is expected to sit between the Galaxy S27+ and Galaxy S27 Ultra. Previous leaks suggest that the phone could feature a more compact design while retaining several premium features from the Ultra, including the Privacy Display. However, unlike the Ultra, the Pro model reportedly won't come with an S Pen.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Update 8:49 p.m. Nov. 13: According to reports, airline sources say the ground stop has been lifted.

It has been revealed that on Friday afternoon, the FAA grounded all planes nationwide, an extraordinary step that brought air travel to a grinding halt. The aviation administration noted it halted travel "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.".

U.S. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy also confirmed the flight stoppage on X.

Sources indicate that "The [FAA] issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication matter impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.".

The FAA rarely halts traffic coast to coast, leaving many travelers with questions about their flight status and the cause of the grounding. Here's what we know so far.

Sources indicate that the FAA's original explanation was that the ground stoppage was necessary "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety." That was a vague and somewhat anxiety-inducing communication, as many Americans associate nationwide ground stoppages with the tragedy of Sept. 11, when flights were also stopped in dramatic fashion.

However, the FAA soon clarified in a statement that the order was issued due to a telecommunications issue.

"There has been a temporary telecommunications outage — out of an abundance of caution, all flights have been halted. Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis.".

However, CNN reported this extraordinary quote, citing an unnamed airline source: "Ten minutes ago, they were on a crisis call and there was still no clear answer as to a cause." More recently, CNN reported that the FAA told airlines that the problem originated with "network routers.".

In a White House press briefing late Friday evening, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin explained the ground stop was the result of outdated air traffic control systems. Duffy stated the analogue systems were "overloaded" by a patchwork of newly-installed modern technology, which caused inconsistencies in radar and communications. The FAA ordered the ground stop out of an "abundance of caution," officials explained.

According to the Misery Map, a visualization of cancellations and delays produced by the flight-tracking service FlightAware, there have been 2,406 delays and 763 cancellations so far today. At the same time yesterday, FlightAware recorded 410 delays and six cancellations.

Because of the chaotic nature of a sudden ground stoppage, many travelers may be stuck sitting in planes on the tarmac. One Mashable reporter is currently in exactly that situation.

In the hours after the FAA grounded all domestic flights, major airports are warning travelers to check their flight status before heading to the airport. The X account of Latest York City's John F. Kennedy Airport wrote, "Travelers should confirm their flight status with their airline before heading to the airport." Dulles International Airport in Washington, DC issued the following advisory to travelers: "Prior to coming to the airport, check with your airline regarding the status of your flight." According to recent reports, the FAA has only grounded all planes nationwide on two prior occasions. It happened for the first time on 9/11, and then again on Jan. 11, 2023. In the latter incident, flights were grounded for just 90 minutes due to issues with the Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) system. In 2024, the infamous CrowdStrike IT outage led major airlines to concern a global stoppage.

According to recent reports, as with yesterday's global Microsoft outage, online commentators rapidly speculated that a cyberattack may have been the cause of the ground stoppage, but there is currently no reason to believe that is the case. The FAA has clearly stated that it's the result of "a temporary telecommunications outage." Mullin reiterated in the Friday briefing that there were "no indications" of foreign interference as of now.

Sources indicate that the FAA's IT infrastructure is notoriously out of date. Just last week, Mashable reported on the administration's plans to finally phase out floppy disks — two years from now.

CBS News reported that multiple sources told them "[a]n update to the private communications network that connects America's air traffic control system caused the system to reboot, leading to a crash and a communications outage." A Florida-based company, L3Harris, operates that system, according to CBS News.

Speaking at a news conference, Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said, "This is not another 9/11," according to KOMO News.

In a recent development, "There is no fear to the public. I want to make sure we say this again — there is no reason for the public to be afraid or scared for your loved ones," the secretary stated.

Sources indicate that in recent days, the FAA confirmed it was expanding the use of an AI tool to help air traffic controllers manage traffic, according to Ars Technica. However, there is no evidence that the current stoppage and the AI rollout are related. That hasn't stopped frustrated travelers from speculating on a connection, however.

On Friday evening, the tech giant behind the newly introduced AI tool stated that there was absolutely no connection between the ground stoppage and its work.

Unfortunately, it's impossible to answer that question. As we already noted, the last nationwide ground stoppage in 2023 lasted approximately 90 minutes, according to the FAA's communications at the time.

If CNN's source who claimed the FAA currently has no idea what caused the problem is correct, it could drag on much longer than travelers would like.

We should also note that it's at the moment Friday the 13th.

Many Redditors have expressed dismay at the launch of Reddit Reviews, a upcoming AI-powered feature which aims to summarise posts about particular products.

Reddit is positioning the feature as a way to save time and effort when researching a potential purchase, but many Redditors say that replacing human interaction with AI summaries is antithetical to the whole philosophy of the platform – and is going to make the existing spam problem massively worse ….

The value of customer reviews on ecommerce platforms like Amazon is becoming increasingly questionable thanks to practices like astroturfing by brands and offering people free products in return for five-star reviews.

In a recent development, that’s led to Reddit becoming one of the most trusted sources of feedback and advice on potential purchases, precisely because it’s a forum in which real people are free to express their true opinions. Indeed, many use a filter in their Google searches to draw content from Reddit specifically, adding the suffix ‘site:reddit.com’.

Recent findings suggest that reddit is increasingly a cesspool of maligned moderators (human and bot) and owners looking to make a bot. Posters on the platform are simply supplying free content with nothing to gain except bans when someone/somebot disagrees with them.

Reddit certainly isn’t immune to astroturfing – that is, fake posts by brands posing as ordinary users – but moderators put a lot of work into deleting spam and other inauthentic posts.

In a recent development, the platform yesterday unveiled the launch of Reddit Reviews, in which AI summarises the posts made about particular products and product categories. It’s being pitched as a way for people to save time when seeking the product opinions of Redditors.

It has been revealed that across Reddit’s communities, people discuss everything from hobbies and daily life to products they’re researching. By offering perspectives grounded in real experience, these conversations provide valuable context in every purchase decision journey […].

Today, we are starting to test Reddit Reviews, a latest experience that organizes product conversations from across Reddit into dedicated reviews and highlights the most key takeaways from across our communities.

However, as CNET spotted, the move has led to a backlash by many Redditors and subreddit moderators.

“I’ve already seen this in practice and it is a nightmare. It turns a basic conversation into an ad-ridden distracting mess. It’s horrible to read and had me fleeing every thread I saw it in.”.

“I am a moderator on a couple of health subs and we explicitly do not allow advertisements because most of them are bullshit slop and completely predatory for vulnerable and newly diagnosed patients. We do not want, or need this, on our subs!”.

“The enshittification continues.”.

“Yeah, this definitely isn’t going to lead to even more fake account stealth marketing efforts across the site.”.

“This is going to make our spam fighting even worse. This is horrible.”.

“Every decision made by Reddit lately encourages spam and/or abuse that will make spam.”.

“Not a single person who uses Reddit wants this.”.

“You are incentivising existing spammers to continue or step up their activities, now that there’s a newly introduced well they can poison.”.

Recent findings suggest that I find it hard to disagree with the view that almost every monetization step the platform has made has degraded the user experience. This seems almost guaranteed to be another one.

  • Sources indicate that the outage debacle began around lunchtime on the East Coast on Thursday, with customers reporting Outlook outages to the service-tracking website Downdetector just after 12 pm ET.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sorry, Margaret, your email is working again.

After a widespread outage shut down Microsoft 365 services for businesses, governments, and tens of millions of other consumers around the world, the essential cloud services are now (mostly) back online, according to the company’s status page.

Sources indicate that the outage debacle began around lunchtime on the East Coast on Thursday, with customers reporting Outlook outages to the service-tracking website Downdetector just after 12 pm ET. Within the hour, Microsoft said it was investigating reports of an outage that at the time was limited to North America. It quickly spread to impact more than 70 countries around the world.

Recent findings suggest that the full cause of Microsoft’s unprecedented outage remains unknown, but the company repeatedly ruled out a cyberattack as the cause in statements to its status page. It is also ruling out AI or AI agents playing a role in the debacle.

Industry observers note that “We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services,” a Microsoft spokesperson indicates in a statement. “This was a technical concern not related to cyber or AI/agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions.”.

The company has promised a “full post-incident report” after it has fully reviewed what went wrong.

According to recent reports, as Outlook, Teams, Copilot, and other Microsoft 365 systems come back online, owners will likely see their inboxes turn into a mess. “You're probably going to get a lot of notifications when things come back,” says Jonathan Leitschuh, an independent researcher.

Microsoft stated it had increased the queue time for emails to 48 hours in an attempt to ensure that every message that people tried to send while its systems were down gets delivered. Leitschuh points out that, even with the bulk of systems restored, customers may receive “a flood of notifications a few hours down the pike” as subsystems come back online.

The total impact of the Microsoft outage may never be fully known, but it’s safe to say it’s already significant. Governments from Japan to the United States reported disruptions to a bevy of functions. Airlines reported problems with their ability to communicate with customers. Many law enforcement and emergency services ground to a halt. And hospitals reported widespread interruptions to their operations.

Sources indicate that ultimately, the episode serves as a reminder of the risks involved when the whole world relies on a single company for a critical service. “We're very interdependent on these systems in modern life,” notes Leitschuh. Next time, delayed emails may be the least of our worries.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • 9), it was reported by Windows Report that Google was finally working on solving a security glitch when browsing in Incognito Mode.
  • The publication pointed out something interesting: while Incognito mode doesn't (currently) offer real-time protections, the browser will "fall back" on its knowledge of dangerous sites stored "locally." But that's as far as its protections go, and in this day and age, it's not good enough.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

All things considered, Incognito Mode in Google Chrome is a useful feature; however, it's not without fault. The company might be trying to solve a key security issue that users have had to endure.

Earlier today (Nov. 9), it was reported by Windows Report that Google was finally working on solving a security glitch when browsing in Incognito Mode. The publication noticed a new Chromium commit, stating that it's working on adding "Safe Browsing protections" for Incognito mode. Essentially, this would bring real-time protections to customers while they're browsing. This is no different from operating Chrome without Incognito active.

The publication pointed out something interesting: while Incognito mode doesn't (currently) offer real-time protections, the browser will "fall back" on its knowledge of dangerous sites stored "locally." But that's as far as its protections go, and in this day and age, it's not good enough.

According to recent reports, additionally, while this is a good thing, the point of Incognito mode is to remain private in your browsing (many aspects don't get logged in your browser). The publication notes that developers are staying aware of this. Developers are working to ensure that privacy-related details about your Incognito session don't leave your device.

There's much for Google to do; however, according to the Chromium commit, it looks like Incognito will benefit from Standard and Enhanced browsing protections—it'll be the user's choice.

Sources indicate that as we've mentioned before, Incognito Mode is supposed to be your gateway to more private browsing. But that wasn't always the case. Google admitted to tracking people while they had the feature active. In 2024, Google settled a class-action lawsuit for $5 billion. The lawsuit alleged that the firm "misled users" into thinking they were privately browsing, meaning tracking wasn't involved.

Google's disclaimer said that it wouldn't save a user's browsing data; however, others (ISPs and websites) could still see it. That disclaimer has since been updated. The manufacturer now states the browser isn't tracking you, but Google still can. This didn't sit well with customers, as you'd imagine. Shortly after, Google said it would delete all of the data it captured about users who had Incognito mode active. This was part of the settlement.

When Apple introduced the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, the manufacturer remarked that it had completely redesigned the cooling system for “incredible sustained performance.”.

That could sound like marketing hype, but a YouTuber has found a great way to let us actually see the upcoming system living up to Apple’s claims ….

The real-life performance of any electronic device depends not only on the power of the chip but a range of additional factors. A key one is the effectiveness of the cooling system, because when the device gets too hot, the performance will be throttled in order to avoid damage.

In the worst of cases, the theoretical maximum performance of a chip is only delivered for a very short time before it is throttled back to a much lower level. Thermal management is absolutely key in the case of a laptop like the MacBook Pro.

Apple noted that the latest model has a completely latest cooling system.

A completely redesigned thermal architecture enables […] incredible sustained performance of M5 Pro and M5 Max, even in a lighter design, while redirecting warm air away from the display.

As Macworld spotted, a YouTuber has found a simple but clever way to enable us to actually see the difference with our own eyes.

A YouTube video by Geekerwan compared the mini-LED MacBook Pro with the new PROLED XDR model using a fog machine. With each MacBook’s fans running, you can clearly see how the internal design disperses the heat: In the old model, heat goes both out and up through the display, while the PROLED pushes the heat toward the back of the device through the hinge.

In a recent development, cooling is particularly challenging when the laptop is closed while connected to an external monitor, and the results of the testing show a dramatic improvement by the latest model. You can watch the video below, which links directly to the demo – but Geekerwan’s videos are always worth watching in full, so click here to watch the whole thing.

Following the preview at the end of last month, Google is now bringing its latest Gemini 4 Carbon model to the Gemini app.

Officially, Google claims “Argon remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work, while Carbon is built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence.” Examples include “complex, multi-step coding and debugging and open-ended scientific research and discovery.”.

In the model picker, 4 Argon is for “Code & analysis” and 4 Carbon is for “Most complex work.” Notably, the Gemini app has removed 3.1 Pro with this launch.

According to recent reports, to showcase performance on larger, more complex projects, Google Antigravity is previewing /swarm. This turns a “single prompt into a coordinated team of agents you can track in real time.”.

Developers can assign Carbon to roles that demand the deepest reasoning, like architectural design, coordination, and auditing, while pairing it with faster, lighter models across parallel isolated workspaces and adversarial verifiers that test every change.

For legal, finance, and enterprise work, Carbon is noted to bring “higher-precision knowledge work, artifact generation, and data analysis.” This includes how the model will follow “strict schemas and formatting to generate polished and precise spreadsheets, presentations, and reports.”.

Existing benchmarks don’t adequately capture how agents reason natively over dense files with charts, images, blueprints, schematics, and tables, so we partnered with Artificial Analysis to launch the latest Multimodal Knowledge Agents (MKA) benchmark. Carbon ranks #1 while using 3X fewer tokens than the next best model across 200 tasks that test a model’s multimodal performance in agentic workflows.

Industry observers note that the introductory pricing for Carbon is $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens until November 30. Afterward, it will cost $4 per 1M input tokens and $20 per 1M output tokens.

Connections is the one of the most popular New York Times word games that's captured the public's attention. The game is all about finding the "common threads between words." And just like Wordle, Connections resets after midnight and each new set of words gets trickier and trickier—so we've served up some hints and tips to get you over the hurdle.

Sources indicate that if you just want to be told today's puzzle, you can jump to the end of this article for today's Connections solution. But if you'd rather solve it yourself, keep reading for some clues, tips, and strategies to assist you.

The NYT's latest daily word game has become a social media hit. The Times credits associate puzzle editor Wyna Liu with helping to create the upcoming word game and bringing it to the publications' Games section. Connections can be played on both web browsers and mobile devices and require players to group four words that share something in common.

According to recent reports, each puzzle features 16 words and each grouping of words is split into four categories. These sets could comprise of anything from book titles, software, country names, etc. Even though multiple words will seem like they fit together, there's only one correct answer.

Sources indicate that if a player gets all four words in a set correct, those words are removed from the board. Guess wrong and it counts as a mistake—players get up to four mistakes until the game ends.

In a recent development, players can also rearrange and shuffle the board to make spotting connections easier. Additionally, each group is color-coded with yellow being the easiest, followed by green, blue, and purple. Like Wordle, you can share the results with your friends on social media.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yesterday brought a surprise move by Apple when it abruptly ceased write access to the Apple Support Community and declared that it would be permanently closing in just over a week.

While the news does make me a little nostalgic, I do have to say that I think its time had long since come and gone ….

As we noted yesterday, the community has a fairly long history. It started in 1998 as the Apple Tech Exchange before being renamed Apple Discussions and finally relaunching as Apple Support Communities in 2011. There were some paid community specialists working for Apple on the forum, while the majority of the responses came from volunteers.

The company’s statement was brief and didn’t give any official explanation for the shutdown.

According to recent reports, the AppleCare Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state.

It has been revealed that interestingly, Verizon did exactly the same thing with its own Community Forum earlier this year, with an immediate switch to read-only access, followed shortly afterwards by closing it altogether. That too had a reasonably long history, having first launched back in 2008.

According to recent reports, I suspect in both cases this was mostly about streamlining operations and reducing costs. CEO John Ternus does seem to be aiming to improve efficiency and eliminate what he views as unnecessary expenses. Additionally, community forums always run the risk of reputational damage when customers criticize decisions made by the firm.

I’m old enough to remember the times when the forum was one of the first places I’d turn when troubleshooting an concern with an Apple product, but in all honesty, that hasn’t been the case for a very long time now. A lot of the suggestions were very basic steps any experienced user would already have tried.

There was sometimes also a snarky tone to some of the responses, essentially amounting to “Apple doesn’t promise you should be able to do X, so why are you expecting to do this?” or “Apple already provides a better way to do Y so use it.”.

If you were very upcoming to Apple devices and needed very basic help, then I’m sure it could sometimes prove useful, but I have to say that for a very long time now my own starting point has always been Reddit. I don’t think too many people are going to mourn the passing of ASC.

Spotify’s flagship AI DJ is like Marmite; users either love it for hands-free playback or hate it for infiltrating music discovery. One thing that both types of users can agree on is how jarring its voiceover can be — but that’s about to change.

Rolling out today (November 10) in markets where AI DJ is available, the in-app tool is getting a slew of fresh voices, allowing you to tailor your playback experience exactly to your liking. It marks AI DJ’s biggest overhaul since the launch of its requests feature in May 2025, and is coming to both Android and iOS.

Industry observers note that there are nine new voices in total, with seven new English-language DJs spanning British, Irish, American, Indian, and Australian accents, as well as two new Spanish-language voice options. Instead of the one bog-standard voice that grates on you after a few listens, each new addition is designed to offer something different depending on how you want the experience to run.

Recent findings suggest that whether that’s a cool, collected tone for laidback listening, or an engaging radio host-style personality for high-energy playback, AI DJ’s new personas seem to cover it all. That remarked, it’s not just the new voices that make up AI DJ’s latest revamp.

When it comes to AI DJ, the interruptions between songs plague consumers just as much as its voice, which is why Spotify is allowing you to toggle off DJ’s extensive commentary between segments in the playback. Though Spotify says you’ll still hear AI DJ’s introduction when you start a session or refresh it with new requests, the experience will be completely commentary-free to put the focus back on the music.

Despite Spotify’s advanced features, AI DJ isn’t my personal favorite, and not just for the reasons mentioned above. That remarked, some of my music-obsessed friends stand by it as an easy way to get your daily listening minutes in, and I think its new voice presenters will be a welcome addition for them in particular.

For starters, most of the new personas seem significantly less intense and in-your-face than Spotify’s existing host, most notably DJ Declan and DJ Nell, who are Spotify’s new Irish and British voices. The same goes for DJ Sam, the Australian presenter.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

Industry observers note that as for the three new American voices, this is where Spotify is sticking with its roots. With the exception of DJ Tess, the ‘direct but inviting’ presenter with a laid-back cadence, DJ Casey and the southern-sounding DJ Lane sound just as jarring as Spotify’s inaugural AI DJ voice.

Spotify is really tapping into its personalization ethos with its latest family of AI DJ personas, and yes, it gives users more choice, but it doesn’t fix the biggest concerns with AI DJ — those being its repetitiveness and hindrance to music discovery as a result.

In a recent development, as you could probably gather, my experiences using AI DJ have been less than thrilling, and hitting the play button just triggers a listening session packed with my most-played songs from the past week or so. The same goes for using it to find fresh artists.

I’m constantly on the hunt for new artists and sounds, but AI DJ doesn’t quite get that. Whenever I request a list of new songs from rising artists based on the music I already listen to, it gives me nothing but tracks from artists that are already on my radar.

Sources indicate that given my tumultuous relationship with AI DJ, there’s no wonder I left it in the dust years ago. Even though Spotify peddles it as a handy music discovery tool, I’ve found more luck with using my Daylist for fresh finds — it’s how I discovered Chappell Roan before the virality kicked in, and I’ve never looked back.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some WhatsApp beta testers on iOS are seeing a fresh option in the app’s bottom navigation bar that replaces the Communities tab. Here are the details.

Over the past few years, WhatsApp has increasingly focused on Communities as more people have turned to messaging platforms to interact in smaller, more private groups rather than through traditional social networks.

At the same time, WhatsApp has been testing several features that make it easier for users to see which of their contacts are online and available to chat.

Back in May, WABetaInfo found that WhatsApp was developing a upcoming Contacts hub that would bring together customers’ favorite contacts, as well as those who were currently online or had recently been active.

A few weeks later, WhatsApp began testing a upcoming green dot indicator on iOS to make it easier to identify contacts who were online.

Now, WABetaInfo reports that WhatsApp is rolling out the latest Contacts hub to some iOS beta testers, replacing the Communities tab in the app’s bottom navigation bar.

The latest tab includes a section with favorite contacts and a full contact list. Users can see their favorite contacts at the top of the screen, making it easier to start a conversation with them. They can also sort the full contact list by activity, alphabetical, and birthdays. With alphabetical, the app organizes contacts by name. With activity, WhatsApp demonstrates who is currently online at the top of the list. WhatsApp marks these contacts with a green dot, so users can easily distinguish them from offline contacts. WhatsApp also sorts recently active contacts by last seen, so users can quickly identify who was active most recently. With birthdays, WhatsApp sorts contacts by their upcoming birthday, so users can see who has a birthday coming up soon.

The site notes that the new tab also allows owners to add contacts directly, with the option to sync them to their iPhone’s address book.

As for Communities, the feature itself isn’t going away, but rather being moved to a dedicated filter in the Chats tab.

WABetaInfo also notes that WhatsApp is experimenting with potentially replacing the Updates tab, rather than Communities, with the Contacts tab in a future configuration.

For now, the latest Contacts tab is available to a limited number of beta testers running the latest WhatsApp beta for iOS via TestFlight, with a broader rollout expected over the coming weeks.

Breaking: FAA Grounds All US Flights Until Further Notice

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (551 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Patch, 8:45 pm EST Friday: The FAA’s ground stop is now over.
  • The Federal Aviation Administration grounded all US flights Friday afternoon, due to “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” the agency stated in a statement.
  • In a post on X, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy mentioned that the ground stop was related to a communication problem affecting Air Traffic Control Centers and agency technicians are investigating.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Patch, 8:45 pm EST Friday: The FAA’s ground stop is now over.

The Federal Aviation Administration grounded all US flights Friday afternoon, due to “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” the agency stated in a statement. Flights already in the air will be allowed to land, the agency said, but no fresh ones are permitted to take off.

In a post on X, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy mentioned that the ground stop was related to a communication problem affecting Air Traffic Control Centers and agency technicians are investigating.

In a recent development, the ground stop came after widespread reports of radio frequency outages among several of the nation’s most critical Air Traffic Control Centers, including in Boston, Chicago, and Latest York. Air traffic controllers use designated radio frequencies to communicate with pilots and manage and monitor airspace safety. In the past, controllers have used voice communications relayed over these radio frequencies to direct traffic; in recent years, the FAA has also rolled out a text-based communication system.

Reached for comment, an FAA spokesperson did not provide any additional details.

Nationwide ground stops are rare. The FAA halted all air traffic on September 11, 2001. In January of 2023, a ground stop was issued after an outage to a critical system that the FAA used to distribute real-time data and warnings to pilots, known as NOTAM (Notice to Air Mission).

In a recent development, “This really points to how much we need to modernize our air traffic control system,” says Susan Hotle, a professor of transportation engineering at Virginia Tech who worked at the FAA. “Right now all it takes is for one system to go out, and it affects a wide region at once.”.

Earlier Friday, Duffy wrote congressional leaders to ask lawmakers to “act swiftly” on the Transportation Department’s request for $30.1 billion funding updates to the nation’s air traffic control system.

Recent findings suggest that if the outage lasts more than a couple hours, it will take airlines—and the flyers that depend on them—days to recover, states Michael McCormick, a professor at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University and a former air traffic controller. An extended stop would mean “airline systems are going to be complete in chaos, with aircraft and air crews in the wrong places. It would take days to get up and back running normally,” he says.

The FAA stated this week that it was rolling out a new AI tool to help advise air traffic controllers. The tool, now available nationwide, had been tested in the busy Washington, DC, region. Air Space Intelligence, the FAA contractor responsible for the tool, posted on X that the groundstop “is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and [Air Traffic Control].”.

At San Francisco International Airport on Friday, hoards of confused travelers lined up to speak with airline staff. A number flights at the airport had already been delayed because of high winds, and the FAA ground stop was now compounding the issue.

It has been revealed that “The FAA has issued a nationwide ground stop,” a United Airlines employee said over the intercom at Terminal 3 near the E departure gates. “This is a nationwide event.”.

Louise Matsakis contributed reporting from SFO.

The FAA nationwide ground stop sparks travel panic and viral memes

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (793 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Enhancement: The ground stop has been lifted, and domestic flights resumed late Friday.
  • history, flights across the United States have been ordered to stay on the ground.
  • 13, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a nationwide ground stop for departing flights following widespread air traffic control communications problems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Enhancement: The ground stop has been lifted, and domestic flights resumed late Friday.

For only the third time in U.S. history, flights across the United States have been ordered to stay on the ground. And as travelers found themselves stranded at airports, sitting in airport bars, and wondering when they might finally take off, the internet did what it does best and started posting.

On Friday, Nov. 13, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a nationwide ground stop for departing flights following widespread air traffic control communications problems. The agency cited extraordinary circumstances and safety concerns, ordering aircraft to remain on the ground until further notice. Flights already in the air were permitted to land, while inbound international flights were being handled on a case-by-case basis.

Recent findings suggest that the scale of the disruption is difficult to overstate. The last time the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop was in January 2023, when a computer system failure temporarily halted departing flights. Before that, it happened in the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

It's the kind of historical comparison that can make an already unsettling situation feel even more alarming, particularly when thousands of travelers are left waiting for answers. The FAA's original communication was also extremely vague, citing only "extraordinary circumstances" and "reasons of safety.".

And on social media, people had plenty of questions.

In a recent development, for travelers caught in the middle of the disruption, the news wasn't just another breaking headline. It meant unexpected delays, uncertain departure times, and an increasingly familiar feeling of being at the mercy of systems entirely outside their control.

Some turned to social media to document the experience in real time, sharing updates from airport terminals.

Others were struck by the sheer rarity of the moment. A nationwide ground stop is not an everyday occurrence, and the fact that the previous two were associated with 9/11 and a major FAA systems failure only added to the unease.

Of course, this being the internet, it didn't take long for people to find humor in the situation, either. Even an unprecedented disruption to air travel isn't immune to a few jokes, particularly when it happens on Friday the 13th following a major Microsoft outage.

And then, there's this response from Stephen King:.

It has been revealed that but beyond the immediate frustration and online commentary, the ground stop raises more serious questions about the aging technology underpinning America's aviation system. The FAA has been working to modernize its air traffic control infrastructure, and Friday's communications problems offer another reminder of how much depends on systems most travelers rarely think about until something goes wrong.

Recent findings suggest that the ground stop also comes at a particularly interesting moment for the FAA. Just days earlier, the agency announced that it was expanding its new AI-supported air traffic management system, known as SMART, to all 22 regional air traffic control centers nationwide. Shortly before that, the FAA announced it will finally phase out floppy disks by 2028.

Industry observers note that the $875 million system is designed to analyze everything from weather patterns and flight routes to traffic congestion and controller staffing, helping aviation officials anticipate disruptions before they happen. According to the FAA, the technology is intended to reduce delays and make air travel more efficient, though human specialists remain responsible for reviewing its recommendations.

The timing has attracted attention online, particularly as questions swirl around what caused Friday's communications problems.

For now, travelers are left refreshing their flight statuses, waiting for updates, and sharing their experiences online. And while the jokes might offer a momentary distraction, there's nothing particularly funny about realizing just how promptly an entire country's air travel system can grind to a halt.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The worst part of owning smart curtain motors is charging them, because it usually means taking the whole motor down from the track or running a really long USB cord to charge it. Today, SwitchBot has released the SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 aimed at solving that problem with a battery module that detaches on its own, so the motor stays in place, and you only take down the part that needs to charge.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

It has been revealed that the SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 is a retrofit motor for curtains that hang on a U-rail track. You hang it on the track between the curtain hooks, run a one-tap calibration in the SwitchBot app, and your existing curtains can then be motorized and used in your smart home. There’s no drilling, no rewiring, and no need to position magnets to stick to the rail, as earlier SwitchBot curtain motors required. SwitchBot claims the whole setup takes about 30 seconds.

One thing to check first: this version is for U-rail tracks only, not curtain rods.

The Battery+ version pairs a small built-in battery with a detachable 5,000mAh module for a total of 6,400mAh. SwitchBot rates it at up to 12 months of use for each charge, depending on curtain weight and movement frequency. When it needs charging, you pull the module off, charge it via USB-C, and clip it back on. SwitchBot also sells a Solar version that uses a small panel to keep the battery topped off if the window gets enough sun.

According to recent reports, the motor itself connects via Bluetooth, so getting it into Apple Home requires a compatible SwitchBot Hub, which brings it there via Matter. Once it’s there, the curtains work like any other window covering in your Home app. You can add them to scenes, control them with Siri, and include multiple windows in a single automation. It’s always nice to time smart curtains/shades with dusk/dawn as well.

SwitchBot’s built-in QuietDrift mode opens the curtains slowly in the morning, at about half a centimeter per second, so the room fills with daylight gradually rather than all at once. SwitchBot claims it runs at around 25 dB in that mode. You can also give the curtain a gentle tug by hand and the motor takes over, which is great if you don’t have your iPhone with you or someone doesn’t have access to your Apple Home setup.

SwitchBot built it in a way to correct drift over time, so you shouldn’t need to recalibrate it if it gets off.

The SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 turns the U-rail curtains you already have into Apple Home window coverings without replacing anything. The detachable battery is the best feature here, as it lets you charge it without a long cord.

The SwitchBot Curtain Track 4 is available now on Amazon and directly from SwitchBot.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google is boosting the Gemini experience with a latest upgrade that's designed to give you more control over how you manage the information the chatbot saves about you.

The new Memory summary tool gives you all the information Gemini has gathered about you from your chatbots, allowing you to edit its summaries to provide additional data or delete things Gemini gets wrong, as spotted by Android Authority.

It's a pretty handy way to tailor your Gemini experience exactly to your liking, but it presents your data in a specific way. Instead of compiling everything Gemini thinks it knows about you into one massive chunk, Memory summary divides your information into distinct sections that cover specific areas.

For example, the Essentials tab functions as a quick one-stop area showcasing your background, location, and key relationships. Gemini also has other other sections for giving you a snapshot of what it remembers about your career, interests, etc, all of which you can chop and change to tailor its knowledge of you more accurately.

Gemini is rolling out a new feature called "Memory Summary"! 🧠✨ This update lets you easily view and edit the key details that Gemini remembers about you. 📝👀 https://t.co/kXO4HjQEanNovember 9, 2026.

In a recent development, however, as helpful as it sounds, Google's support page states Memory summary is right now available to consumers in the US with an active Google AI proposal who are over the age of 18, and it needs Keep Activity and Memory enabled to work. According to the manufacturer, it's also restricted to English-only, and it's unclear whether Google will expand its language availability.

But despite the apparent limitations Google lists, it doesn't seem to be the case with Gemini's web version. That stated, Memory summary appears to be working for some free users on web and mobile browsers, but not in the Gemini mobile app. We've tried to access Memory summary on Gemini's web and mobile browser versions, but have had no luck so far.

As far as finding it goes, it's quite simple. Head to Gemini and tap the Settings icon, then tap Personal Intelligence and then Memory summary. It's available in both the Gemini app and web browser, though it won't appear in the former unless you're based in the US and signed up to a Google AI strategy.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Moon is getting a little bit bigger each night as we work through the lunar phases.
  • Industry observers note that as of Saturday, Nov.
  • If you don't have any visual aids, you can see see some features on the Moon's surface tonight, specifically the Mare Crisium and the Mare Fecunditatis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Moon is getting a little bit bigger each night as we work through the lunar phases. We're still in the Waxing Crescent phase, which means more of the Moon is becoming illuminated each evening as it makes its way towards the First Quarter.

Industry observers note that as of Saturday, Nov. 14, the NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waxing Crescent phase, with 22% of its surface visible.

If you don't have any visual aids, you can see see some features on the Moon's surface tonight, specifically the Mare Crisium and the Mare Fecunditatis. With binoculars or a telescope, you'll also see the Endymion Crater.

The next Full Moon will take place on November 24.

According to recent reports, the Moon takes approximately 29.5 days to complete one full cycle. As it orbits Earth, the amount of sunlight reflecting off its surface that we can see changes, creating the different phases. This takes us from the Upcoming Moon to the Full Moon and back again, before the cycle begins once more, according to NASA.

Fresh Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).

Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).

It has been revealed that first Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.

Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.

In a recent development, waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere).

Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.

Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake now runs surprisingly well on phones after just a week of additional emulator development.

Legend of Zelda fans all over the world have been marveling at the Ocarina of Time remake’s visuals and enhanced gameplay systems on the Nintendo Switch 2, but the Android emulator scene has been busy marveling over something just a little bit different. One Redditor got the latest Zelda game running on Banana Native, a free emulator that’s available right now on GitHub.

Recent findings suggest that ocarina of Time remake performance has now reached a major milestone into the 30 FPS territory with frame gen, which means the game is actually running at around 15 FPS, but then scaled and interpolated using AI frame generation to appear like 30 FPS. Banana Native isn’t a traditional emulator, as it doesn’t emulate hardware. Rather, it uses the game’s own ARM64 code to run on the phone’s CPU. The Switch 2 is powered by a mobile Nvidia chip, after all.

According to recent reports, the user is running the Ocarina of Time remake on a Poco F7 Ultra, which sports a two-generation-old Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite (Gen 4) processor. The latest phones that are coming out, like the Redmagic 12 Pro, run a 6th-gen Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme chip, so performance could be a lot better on a newer phone. Apps like Banana Native require specific driver support for each phone to run, and as I pointed out in my Redmagic 12 Pro review, platforms like Droid Deck and Game Native don’t yet have proper drivers for the newest chips.

In a recent development, 9to5Google’s Damien Wilde recently reviewed Droid Deck, another native-type emulator that lets you legally play Steam games you own on your phone by just signing into your Steam account. It works extremely well on lots of Android phones and helps showcase just how far Android emulation has come this year.

Latest Update: The FAA Nationwide Ground Stop Is Over
